div.head: VLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: VLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

AN OLD MAID'S CONUNDRUM.—To what Was the Wisdom of Solomon due? It was due to the fact that he had seven hundred wives, whom he con- sulted on all occasions. CHEAP.—" What do you propose to take for your cold?" said a lady to a sneezing gentleman, who responded: "ot, I'll cell it very cheap. I ' won't higi4le about the price at all." A NEW SOCIETY.—The last society spoken of in California is the "Pay-Nothing." it is said to be alarmingly prosperous. The password is "Lend us a dollar ;" the response, " Broke." A SELFISH Californian minister recently refused to perform a marriage service where the bride was his own absconding wife. And that aggravating woman said he "was just as mean as he always used to be." "I'm afloat, I'm afloat I" screamed ayoung lady, with powerful lungs and fingers to match, as she exercised both at a piano. " I should think you were," growled an old bachelor, "judging from the squall you raise." A MAN with a large family Was complaining of the difficulty of supporting all of them. "But," said a friend, "you have sons big enough to earn something now." "The difficulty is, toey are too big to work," was the answer. SHE was a crank on the subject of music. A gentlemen knocked at her door and.a.sked:—"Does Mr. Smith live here ?'"' No, sir, his room is an octave higher—in the next fist," she replied, in a pianissimo andante tone of voice. THE Troy Times tells of a gentleman who was awakened in the night and told that his wile was dead. He turned over, drew the coverlet closer, pulled down his nightcap, and murmured, as he went to sleep again, "Oh 1 how grieved in the morning 1" SOCIAL SUILGERY.—A physician has invented knife that cuts so fast that nobody can feel it. After all, however, there is nothing vastly new in this surgical invention. People in society cut each 'other every day, a.nd if they are at all fast neither of them feels it. PUTTING FOOT IN ITALY. —A distinguished lawyer was lately explaining to his son, Who was quite a boy, the outlines of Italy, and remarked, as usual, that they resembled in form a man's boot. "Well," said the little fellow, "if I live to be a man I'll put my foot in it 1" TEE PLAGUE OF THE WARDROBE.—" Moths !" exclaimed an old lady—conning over a string of advertisements relative to a book about those insects—" and where to find them. Where, indeed! AB if there wanted a book written to tell us that,—drat the good-for-nothing, destructif, mischevious things 1" A PHILADELPHIA,N and one of the largest hews. paper advertisers in the country knows a good thing when he sees it. He says: "I confine the advertising of my soap to the newspapers, because the man wko does not read the newspapers does not use soap." A BISHOP, reproving his delinquent page, said, "Wretched boy! who is it that sees and hears all we do, and before whom even I am but a crushed worm ?" The boy replied, "The miasma, my lord !" His lordship said that was not the right answer.

A ritinsr was once called to pray over the barren fields of his parishioners. He passed from one enclosure to another, and pronounced his benedio- tion until he came to a most unpromising case. He surveyed the sterile acres in despair. "Ah !" said he, "brethren—no use to pray here—this needs manure." . T. P. BARNITM told this story ahout himself in his address of welcome to the delegates to the Con- necticut Universalist Convention in Bridgeport:— "An old clergyman once said to me, `Mr. Barnum, I hope to meet you in heaven.' I answered, You will, if you are there.' " A EALF-CRAZED lad in a Northern town named Robert one day presented himself at the counter of a confectioner's shop in the town, and inquired the price of a pound of grapes. "A shilling," replied the shoprnan. "Gie's a penny turnip, then, for I'm awzu' fond o' fruit. SEILGEANT-MAJOII—" Now, Private Smith, you know very well that none but officers and non- commissioned officers are allowed to walk across this grass!" Private Smith—" But, Sergeant- Major, I've Captain Graham's verbal orders to Sergeant-Major—" None o' that, sir! Show Inc the captain's verbal orders I Show 'l7O, to me, sir I"

BAGS OF MYSTERY.—In a case heard at the Tomos police-court a young woman had obtained some saveloys (a kind of dried sausage,) from a pork-butcher under false pretences. The magistrate asked whether saveloys were not a kind of sausage. A voice in the court replied, "Your Honour, they are bags of mystery." A REPORTER, in describing the return of a poli- tician to his room, says: "Entering with the key in his hand, he shut the door and put it in his pocket." On this the Boston Post remarks: "This assertion is certainly false, for he either did not shut the door, or else he did not put it in his pocket. After a campaign has closed there is no excuse for this sort of thing." MRS. PETERBY . hired Matilda Snotspall as a cook, but in about.a week she had oacasion to say to her—" When I hired you you said you didn't have any male friends coming around, and now I find a man in the kitchen half the time." "Why, ma'am, bress your soul, dat man ain't no male friend ob mine. .11e am only my husband," was the reply. "AND who was ,present when you were assaulted by the prisoner" inquired the magistrate of the complainant, a citizen of the city which Mr. Parnell represents in Parliament: "Who was prisint, your worship?" returned the true son of Erin "who was prisint during the assault, is it! Well, then, bedad, your worship, I was prisint myself."

"Well, said the persevering governess, "I will pat it in another shape. If it takes one servant nine hours to do the entire housework of one family, how long will it take .three servants to do it ? ' Little Nell—" Oh, I can answer that. I heard mamma speak of it this morning." Teacher— " Well, how long will it take them ? " Little .Nell—" Three times as long." A GENTLEMAN entered a Chicago gun store, and asked to be showed some revolvers. "Here is a nice family weapon," said the clerk. "family weapon ? ' "Yes, a family weapon. Just the thing for domestic tragedies. It has six chambers, sir. Two bullets for your faithless wife, two for the ruthless destroyer of your home, ,aud two for yourself. They are all the go now." ,A COUNTRY gentleman, going his rounds ilme evening, saw a great snake coiled up on his garden walk. He immediately got an axe, cut the creature into a hundred pieces, returned to his house, told everybody about his exploit, and went to bed. Next morning his gardener came in great tribu- lation to complain that some scoundrel had been in the night and cut to pieces his hest garden hose.

OIIT CYHis Cour.su.—A steamboat captain on Lake Huron was feeling his way in the dark, when the look-out ahead cried out: "Schooner without .a light." It was a narrow escape; and as the ateaer passed the schooner the captain demanded: " That are you doing with your schooner here in the dark without a light!" To his dismay, the skipper, who was a Frenchman, answered.: " Vat diable you do here viz your ole steamboat in three feet of watt*, eh IP" and jast then the steamer landed high and dry on a sand-bank. ONA Of the clergy of a large Scotch town having been ruFalizing, was returning home from a day's piscatorial enj.iyment, his rod across his shoulder, when he met a youth with whom he was slightly acquainted, who happened to be carrying a bridle In his band- The (trine, thinking to be witty, even at the risk of being personal, 'pointed Bignifi_ cantly to the bridle, and, with a shake of his -head and a smile, remarked in passing "A bridle for the ass" to which the young man, nothing daunted, and pointing to the fishing-rod over the clerical shoulder, instantaneously rejoined; " And A rod for the fool's tack." A MAN in Indiana, on returning home from a business journey recently, found that his wife, Zuring his absence, had raffled all the furniture and departed, and the Sheriff arrested him for allow. ing gambling on his premises.

" CAPITAL " CHAT. The award of the University prize essays and poems at Oxford this year is notj2ceable not only for the absence of any Balliol man from the list of successful candidates, but also for the fact that Lord Warkworth, the grandson of the Duke of Nor- thumberland and future successor to the dukedom, has gained the English verse—almost the only ex- ample of a nobleman being suscessful in this com- petition.

Mr. Avon, the Noeconformist master of the Hersham School, Walton-on-Thaires, whose parse- secution at the hands of the lanai Church party has been noticed from time to time, has resigned his position. He goes forth to seek a livelihood in some more tolerant plaee where bigots will permit him to earn and eat his bread in peace. Thus the Church Spreads the Christian virtues. " And the greatest of these is charity."

1 Naples (writes a Correspondent) has seldom seen a more beamtitul springtime than , the one we are now enjoying, and the inEux of visitors is very great, all the hotels being crowded. I am sorry to say that;our International Hospital has just suffered a great loss in the death of its now matron, Miss ,Bdith Green, who had only entered on her duties scarcely two months ago, and has been carried off after a short illness.

Madame Sarah Bernhardt has.rcturned to France from the United States after an absence of 19 'months. As she descended the czngway from the steamer at Have it was noticed that she carried a small cardboard box under her arm. A reporter of I a Paris paper who went on board to meet her was told that this box contained a little of the sand of America. Madame Bernhardt,who looks well, and has come back stouter, played no few than 396 times on her tour. " La 'roses' was given 300 times. Of " Cleopatra" there were 96.rtpresentatious.

" If I may venture;reaid Mr:Balfour in his speech on Saturday .evening at the Royal Academy dinner, "'to parody a phrase ence uttered by a great prelate, now deceased, I think it is better Englishmen should be free than Englishmen should be re sthetic.' The great prelate was the late Archbishop Magee, who died just a year ago. The phrase parodied was "I would rather see England tree than England sober." It was used in denouncing local option. The same prelate is responsible for this equally unhappy phrase. "No State could be goyerned for ten minutes on Christian principles."

IMr. Robert Walsh, the Crown rrosecutor at Mel- bourne, who has woven a halter round the neck of Mr. Deeming, is a big, black-bearded, bright-eyed, good-humoured Iriskiman, who has been practising at the Victoria Bar for .more than a quarter of a rdentury. He went into politics for a time,and held ' the Attorney-Generalship in the Ministry of Sir 'Charles Cavan Duffy. But he found Parliamentary Itfe and midnight sittings uncongenial, and so wisely devoted himself to hardwork in the courts ty day and domestic bliss in the evening.

He has one peculiarity. Hehas been wearing the same wig for thirty years. .He brought it from Ireland with him when be emigrated to Australia. As a result of long wear and tear it is a most disre- putable headpiece, and it would be difficult to des- cribe its precise color. One day he and Mr. Purves, were on opposite sides in a case for damages arising out of a railway smash, in which color- blindness was pleaded. Mr. .Purves was cross- examining an alleged expert on color-blindness,and suddenly asked him, "What is the color of my learned friend's wig?" "White, of course," promptly replied the expert. "indeed ! " retorted Mr. Purves, " I would be inclined to call it pie- bald."

The Prince of Wales went over to the Marl- berough Club on Tuesday, which was almost his first semi-public appearance in England since the death of the late Duke of Clarence. De looked extremely well. The air of the Riviera has evi- dently agreed with him. Sorrow.has not reduced his weight—his face has recovered its cheerful empression. The Prince and Princess will not be long in England. for they are shortly going to Den- mark to stay with the King and :Queen for the quiet celebration of the golden wedding, which,but for the death of the Duke of Clarence, would have been the occasion of a national rejoicing.

Sir Edward Birkbeck had an encouraging year's work to report at the annual meeting of the National Lifeboat institution on Saturday. A reeo- lui ion lies been passed by the House of Commons in favor of completing electrical .communication between lifeboats and signal stations around the coasts. Sir M. Hicks-Beach told the meeting that the Government were "sensible of the duty imposed upon them," and that they would carry out the work thoroughly. The south coast about Folkestone is now better provided with lifeboats, .but, as we said at the time of the Benvenue disaster, ourlife-saving machinery will not be complete until-it is tore than a purely voluntary organisation depending on public subscription. It should be organised by the • State.

Mrs. Osborne is free again. Mr. Matthews has been kinder to her than even her friends expected. Her nine months' imprisonment have been short- ened to seven weeks. It may be that her, release was necessary owing to the state of her health, but we cannot forget that the Home Secretary, who has an ear for appeals from Mrs. Osborne's aristocratic friends, is callous to all demands made on behalf of Fanny Gene. Mrs. Osborne's sentence was very iii- adequate. and Fanny Gene's was altogether too severe. Indeed it is very doubtful whether she should have been convicted at all. But she is only a pcor domestic servant, and Mr. Matthews is deaf to appeals on her behalf, although he exercises his powers with great promptitude to release the. con- vict Osborne.

Despite the pessimistic rumours concerning the Dockers' Union, Secretary Ben Tillett and the report for last year, which he has just issued, •" in every sense satisfactory." The union is not what it was in 1890, but this could hardly have been ex- pected. Depression of trade, especially the decline in the shipping business, has affected it. Mr. Til- lett says that—" In view of the great depression in trade, the relentless manaiuvring on the part of the employers, the number of strikes occasioned by employers attempting reductions, together with the leaden apathy of many who have been benefited materially; in spite of all this, we have emerged trom the struggle much more effective in our organisation, with a firmer grip of the situation, and a more generous judgment and vigorous resolve to be equal to the responsibilities our work entails;" The strike pay for last year has been £lO,OOO more than in 1890. Mr. Tillett does not tell us the mem- bership, hut there is a decline of £3,100 in the income—from £24,000 to £18,900. The cost of management has increased by 2 per cent.

May the First this year has been productive on the Continent of a great deal of pictorial literature of satiric or emblematic design. Some of the best productions are by one of our own countrymen, Mr. Walter Crane, who has designed a female character with wings, supposed to represent the Paris Corn- ' mume of 1871,and an allegorical procession,crammed ' with figures, showing the "Triumph of Labour." These are in Mr. Crane's characteristic style, and are published at Zurich. The Dutch Socialists issue an allegory of a lot of swine feeding, and preventing other swine, who are outside some barriers, from • getting to the troughs. This is "Constitutional Monarchy," or a "Bourgeoise Republic," which in the artist's mind, are synonymous, whereas, in the coming era of a "Social Republic." which is here foreshadowed, every pig eats out of a long trough nicely divided into compartments, so that each has a compartment all to himself. The suggestion is vague as a guide to a more equal distribution of wealth, but not vaguer,perhaps,than the suggestions of most Socialist speakers. In France, M. Constans is seen sowing bullets at Fourmies, and reaping corn with ears in the likeness of M. Lafargue ; and in Germany, Lassalle and Karl Marx are the subjects of pictorial eulogy. •

THE
SL HELENS TRA.NSFER SESSIONS.
--- - A FOOTBALL PLAYER AND HIS LICENSE.

_ Alderman D. Gamble, C.B, Alderman V. Cook and Mr. A. Sinclair, sat at St. Helens Police Court on Monday, for the purpose of hearing applications for the tranfer of the follewing licenses :—Queen's Vaults, Bridge-street, from William Anthony to Richard Glover; Baths Hotel, Warrington New- road, from Richard Midgeley to John Alker ; Bull's Head Inn, Parr Stooks, from the late Ralph Unsworth to Mrs. Esther Unsworth ; Soldier Inn, Peasley Cross-lane' from the late Samuel Mee to Joseph Bull; Same Place Again Inn, Baldwin-street, from the late Joseph Battersby to Mrs. Ann Battersby:; Seven Stars Inn, Tontine-street, from the late Edward Larkin to Mrs. Larkin; an off- license, Elephant-lane;from John Rigby to William Brown and the Red Lion Inn, 'Robin's-lane, Sutton from James Baldwin to James 'Pilkington, late captain of the St. Helens Recreation Football Club. In regard to the latter application, Chief Constable Wood asked that the matter might be allowed to stand over until the next transfer day, as he was not satisfied with Pilkington's character. He onlylbeard certain information on Satur- day, and he had not had time to make sufficient in- quiries.—Mr. H. L. 'Riley, solicitor, said he appeared for Pilkington when the application for a temporary authority was made three weeks ago, and he then pro- duced the highest testimonial from Messrs. Pilkington Bros., by whom hsehad been employed for about a dozen years. If the Chief Constable had any objection it could only be in reference to matters that did not affect Pilkington keeping a license.—Chief Constable Wood said it was true that lilkington came into court on the former occasion with a certificate from his em- ployers, Messrs. 'Filkiogton Bros., and it was upon that certificate that he get a temporary autho- rity. Bat on Saturday last he (Mr. Wood) was told 'something he had not had sufficient time to inquire into, and he asked that the matter might be adjourned until the next transfer day.—Mr. Riley : About what you have heard of the man there need be no secrecy, as it does not affect his fitness to hold a license. Some girl had accused him in her imagination, which has led her to make similar charges against other people, including an esteemed member of our borough force, which has been indignantly repudiated, of being the father of her child. Even if it were true that Pilkington was the father of the child, your worships will not take it into account.—Chief Constable Wood said he was informed that Pilkington had recently got five women into trouble ; if so he was not fit tohold a license. Mr. Riley.—How are you going to try it'? 'lf five women had got orders against him, perhaps an extremely abnormal case of that sort might have Come weight.—Chief Constable Wood; But I ask for it to .be adjourned until the next transfer day to make some inquiries.—Mr. Riley : I never heard of such a thing before. It is only putting him to expense and trouble, and it is mere rumour by a woman who has made groundless charges against other people.— Mr. Sinclair, J.P. : Are not proceedings being token in the case?—Mr. Riley : The proceedings are being taken out on our side for slander. The girl is not taking proceedings. The Chairman : Does Pilkington mean to work at anything else ?—Mr. Riley: Noo he has thrown up his situation in order to take the house.—The magistrates then retired, and on their re- turn it was stated that all the applications had been granted with the exception of that by Pilkington.—The Chairman 'said the Bench could not see their way to grant the transfer that day.—Mr. Riley asked the magis- trates to renew their temporary authority to Pilkington until the next transfer day, and that would give time to the Chief-constable to make his ioquiries.—The Chairman Yes. ; that is granted.

JACK BRIGGS IN AUSTRALIA. Cricketers in general, but more especially in Widnes, will hail with satisfaction the succcess of this popular cricketer during the recent tour of Lord Sheffield's team in Australia. From the aver- ages which have just been published, Briggs in the batting department occupies a prominent position, having in the representative matches an average of 20 15 for 13 innings, his highest score in one match being 91. For all matches his aggregate decreases to 15 61 for 42 innings, these being the largest numbers indulged in by any member of the team. Briggs figures more promi- nently in the bowling department, for in the representa- tive matches he is second in the averages, his 32 wickets having cost 419 runs, or an average of 13.09, Attewell coming first with 13.02. In all matches played by the team, Briggs comes out with flying colours heading the list in the bowling averages with 140 wickets for 1,073 runs, or an average of 7.66. His most remarkable per- formance in this line was in the last 'match against Australia, when he took 12 wickets for 136 runs, England winning the engagement by an innings and 230 runs.

div.head: LORD -CHANCELLOR IN THE STOCKS.
div.p: A LORD -CHANCELLOR IN THE STOCKS.

The year before he was raised to the Chancellor- ship, Eldon was staying at Lord Dacre's seat, Hoo Park, in Hertfordshire. On a summer afternoon he was walking In a neighbouring village with a country magistrate who was also on a visit to Lord Dacre. Speakin of the stocks and the pillory, he said that he had often sent men to the stocks, and he lied often seen maen in,and he wondered whether they were so very unpleasant as some people aver- red. He thought,not. When his friend said he had a key in his pocket, and asked him if he would like to try what the effect of the stocks was, he said,after seeing the lanes was clear,that he thought he would for a short time. Now, his friend, un- fortunately,. was of an absent mind, and he had scarcely left the Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas when his thoughts reverted to some other subject in which he was deeply in- terested, and he wandered up the 1100 Park. Great was the shock when he was asked where he had left his friend, and the fleetest servant was despatched with the key to release the Chief Justice, who returned to Hoo not, it is said, in the best cf humours, for .while he was in durance, the tale goes, some market carts slowly rambled back from the market, and much regret was expressed to see one so well babited in such a place. In great anger he called out to them he was the Chief Jus- tice of Common Pleas, and some of them must at once get him free, even if they broke the stocks ; but what was his horror when he heard them say that it was shocking to see so very well-dressed a man in such a statel
from

it is said that the tale was kept quiet until there happened to be a trial for some illegal committal to the stocks, and the .safferer brought an action against the bench of justices. For the defence the counsel, who was a “setjeant," claimed only id. damages,as the stocks were merely a slight and not always an unpleasant refuge, the prisoner being surrounded often by friends and sitting in warm Sunshine, &c. ; till the judge interrupted him with "Brother, were you ever in the stocks ?'' "Certainly Uot," was the astonished ,reply. " Ah, well! I thought as much," the judge said; "I have been." -s--" Rambles Round Rugby," by Alfred Ritnmer.

div.head: UNCOMFORTABLE LODGINGS.,
div.p: UNCOMFORTABLE LODGINGS.,

To be lost in an unknown country with a storm coming on is a dangerous and uncomfortable situa- tion. Only a hunter familiar with woodland craft, and possessed of courage and hardihood, can hope to escape death or serious misfortune. A hunter who had lived for many years among the Indians went out on a beaver hunt and got separated from ' his companions. The snow fell thick and the wind blew violently when he tried to End his way back to camp, and he was soon compelled to admit to himself that return was impossible. lie says: As I had only a how, arrows, and tomahawk with me, and no way to strike fire,! was in a dismal situa- tion; and as the air was dark with snow I had little more prospect of steering my course than I should have had in the night. At length I came to a hollow tree, with ahole at one side that I could get into. I went in, and found the place not only dry, but about three feet in diameter and high enough for me to stand in,while a considerable quantity of soft rotten wood lay at the bottom. I concluded to lodge here for the night. With ray tomahawk I chopped off the branches of a fallen tree, set them against the opening,until I had it several feet thick all round,with the exception of a space left to creep in. Then I prepared a block that I could pull in after me to stop this hole. When I went in I took my tomahawk and cut down all the dry, rotten wood I could get, and beat it small. With this I made a tied like a goose nest, and with the small sticks stopped every hole, until my house was dark. I took off nay moccasins and danced in the centre of my bed for about half an hour, till my feet and whole body were agreeably warmed. The snow in the meantime had stopped all the holes, so the place was dark as a dungeon ; though I knew it could not yet be dark out of doors. I coiled up in my blanket and had a fair night's rest. When I awoke all was dark. I coald hear the storm still raging, and concluded I would remain where I was. After a while I tried to find the door, and as I had nothing but the sense of feeling to guide me, the operation took some time. At last I found the block, but it was heavy, and so much snow had fallen on it that I could not move it. I was terrified. Of all the hardships I had ever endured, this seemed the worst. I worked desper- ately, and at length, after what seemed hours of effort I made my way out of the den. The only guide I had by which to steer my way was the trees, as the mess generally grows on the north-west side of them, if they are straight. I went on slowly, and towards night came in sight of camp.

div.head: BLASTING ACCIDENT AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: THE BLASTING ACCIDENT AT HAYDOCK.

DEATH OF A BRAVE MINER. The St. Helens police on Tuesday reported to the county coroner, Mr. Brighouse, the death of Richard Gill, aged filty, of 21, Orrell-street, Parr, St. Helens. The circumstances connected with tile injuries received by Gill were published nineteen or twenty months since. Gill and three other men were Wast- ing in a shaft at the King Pit, Haydock, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. They had four shots rammed and ready to fire. Deceased was in charge of them, and told the men to get into the hoppet as he was firing the shots. He lighted the fuse connected to the four shots, and then got into the hoppet to the men. Almost immediately he said to them," I have given the wrong signal," and he again jumped out of the hoppet to cut off the fuses. He managed to cut one off, but the others were too far burned to allow him to do so. The other men begged Wm to give the signal to ascend, and get into the hoppet, bat he said. *4 No, I will stay where I am. It is better for one man to die than for all." Just then the cage began to ascend, and as it was doing so, the men heard the three shots go off. They were drawn safely to the top, and socn afterwards Gill,who had been unconscious, but who had recovered, pulled the signal wire. They went down to him, and found that he had been badly injured about the head. He was brought up, and taken to the Ilaydock Cottage Hospital, where he remained five months, and was at- tended by Dr. Hayward, who took a piece of stone from off the brain underneath the broken skull. A silver plate was put in the head of the unfortunate man, who eeemed to be getting better, and was sent to the Convalescent Home at Southport. He came back again to St. Helens, but his health failed, and he died on Monday night. It is stated that Gill had no need to get out of the hoppet to cut off the fuses, as he had given the right signal for ascending, but this statement will ,no doubt be inquired into by the coroner. An effort was made to get a Gover- ment award for Gill on account of his bravery, hut this was not successful,and while recognising his heroic con- duct, the Home Secretary did not think it came within the class of cases which merited the grant.

"ELEVEN MEN FROZEN TO DEATH:" " They had wandered round and round in the blinding snowstorm hopelessly lost, in a place only a hundred yards square; and when cold and fatigue vanquished them at last, they seooped oat a rave in the snow and lay down and died, not knotviizg that five steps more would have brought them into the true path." Thus eleven precious lives were lost in making the descent from Mont Blanc in September, 1870. They suffered the bitterest death recorded in the history of those mountains, full as that history is with dreadful tragedies. Sad to think that they were so near safety, and yet through ignorance so far from it. Alas ! how, many die, under different conditions, but for a like reason.
Here is a man who says, "ill my friends thought I was doomed, and I did not care whether I lived or died."

He explains as follows : "Up to October, 1885," he says, "I was a strong, healthy man, and equal to any kind of work. At this time I was taken with a pain that seemed to shoot straight through my heart. I felt as if something was squeezing my heart, and I was in dreadful agony. I had to abandon work and lie up. Then I fell into a low, weak way. I had no appetite, and every morsel I ate gave me a great pain at the chest and a tight, uncomfortable feeling as if all my food turned to wind and did not pass my stomach. I had a great pain at my back and sides, and Wag never free from pain night or day. Such food as I was able to take lay like a load on my stomach, and my heart would thump so badly I could get no sleep, and night after night I would lie awake. "I became that weak I dare not lift the lightest article, and so nervous that the slightest sound staxtled me. Even the children's noise at play upset me. When I ventured out of doors I had to often stand and rest, and my legs were so unsteady I could not walk straight. All this told on my spirits, for before my attack, I scarcely knew my strength. I could lift a sack of flour with ease. " I went to our doctor, who said mine was a bad cases He gave me medicines, but I got not relief from them. Now better, now worse, but never well, I remained in this state for over twelve months, and was under the doctor all that time. At last the doctor recommended me to go to Norwich Hospital and put my-self under a celebrated physician there as an indoor patient. I did so in November, 1886. The physician said, 'Your heart is strained and very weak.'

"Whilst in the hospital I was examined by three doctors, and after being under treatment fine weeks my case was pronounced incurable. The doctors said I would never be able to do hard work again and would never get any stronger. I was now anxious to get home, so I left the hospital, but kept on receiving medicine as an outdoor patient for three months longer. Getting weaker and weaker, I gave up taking their medicine and tried different medicines my friends told me of, but nothing did any good, and I lingered on month after month. Now, indeed, I began to desp•iir, for from a strong, powerful man I was reduced almost to a shadow and did not care whether I lived or died.

" In June, 1837, a book was left at my house which described a preparation called Mother Seigel' Syrup, and I read of one case like mine being cured by it. I said to my wife, 'Here is a case that exactly corresponds with my case.'

" I had lost all faith in medicines, but as a last resource sent to Mr. Edgerley, Supply Stores, Bungay, for a bottle, and had not taken more than half the con- tents before I felt bettet. Wife,' I said, " / believe this Seigel's Syrup is going !o.cul:e _ _

" I began to eat and the food did me good, and I grew stronger and stronger. After taking three bottles I got back to my work strong and healthy, and since then I have never looked behind me. By taking an occasional dose I keep in good ..health. I can now eat anything and do any kind of work, arid went through harvesting as well as anyone, and can lift a pig with ease. I thank God that Seigel's Syrup was evei made known to me, and feel that I owe my life to it. You are at liberty to publish this statement, as I am willing to, tell anyone of the benefit I have derived from the medicine. " Yours truly, I(Signed) "Ma. ROBERT WRIGHT, -• Earsham, B..mgay, Norfolk." " Witness : (Signed) ISAAC WRIGHT,
, "Grocer and Tea Dealer, EArsham."

Mr. Wright's complaint was indigestion and dyspepsia, and the heart (' tithance which so alarmed him was the result of the meehanical pressure of the stomach against the heart when the latter was inflated with the gases created by undigested and unfermenting food. Many are misled thus to mistake indigestion for some other malady. We can only say we are glad our friend found the true path (the right medicine) before Lis disease left him no remnant of life to blow into a flame.

div.head: CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
div.p: THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," " 1171,..re the North Wind Blows," &c., &c.
CILIPTER. XXXVIIL THE GUILTY MAN.

Bill Widdrington's hours were numbered. The injury he had sustained proved to be a very serious one; affecting the spine, producing paralysis of the lower limbs, and giving rise to a numbness and a sensation of intense cold; which, when it once crept up to and reached the heart and vital organs, would inevitably cause death. The doctor warned Bell of this, and suggested that she—as the quietest and most composed of his nurses—should break the sad news to him. Beyond a sudden, sharp drawing in of the breath, the girl showed no visible sign of emotion; and the doctor left congratulating himself upon having evi- dently hit upon the proper person to communicate the hopeless tidings. "His wife is a silly 'hysterical little woman, and really I don't know what I would have done if I'd had to break it to him myself," he mused, as he jogged along on his pony, "but that girl, that sister of his, she's got nerves of steel, I should say! Perhaps lack of feeling though; yes, that is very probable. These fisher-folk are a coarse, brutal sort of people;; though clannish enough all the same .1" It was of course no lack of feeling that gave Bell this suprema self-command. Ever since Bill's acci- dent she had not known any peace of mind. She had never been able to hope much. One thing troubled her greatly. While she had been, nursing her brother, night and day, she had grown aware of one fact—that he had something on his mind ; something that preyed upon him and drove sharp pangs of remorse Into his soul.

What was it? She longed to question, yet she feared to know. But now that his hours were numbered there was no time to lose. If he had sinned, he must be assured that the black gulf of eternity lay before him, and into it he must leap perforce, whether he wished it or no—then let him choose to do so with- out his load of unconfessed guilt lying heavily upon his conscience. She took the opportunity pre- sented by Ailsie's absence during the afternoon, to acquaint Bill with the doctor's hat. There was no one save himself within the cottage; and the sound of the tall clock, ticking in the kitchen, seemed intolerably loud, as she waited to hear how her brother took it. He was so young: so gay, so full of life and energy. It must be bitterly hard to such a one to be snuffed out with no warn- ing, like the flame of an unneeded candle. To her amazement, he accepted the verdict without a allurnmr.

"I'm sick of it, Bell ! sick of ma' life, if it's always to be like it's been this last two months !" "Ye have something' that bothers ye, an' whims let ye rest?" asked Bell. The sick man beckoned her to approach. ." Come thee ways here, an aw'll tell thee what troubles me ;" he said, in a hoarse, broken voice, "if aw had it off my mind, niebbe aw'd dee easier —since it seems aw mun dee ?"

"What ails thee, ma canny lad ?" asked his twin sister, going close up to the bed and speaking softly, as though cooing to a sleepy child; " thou's done now't amiss that aw ken of, but thou munna talk about deeM' afore Ailsie, chance thou breaks her heart ?"
"Poor Ailsie'Twas for her aw kept it dark— only for her, mind ye that, an' (Enna be—ower— hard—o' me lass?"
Me hard! Na, na, Bill, thou's never found me that, anyway! Oot wiv' it, whatever it is. Mak a clean breist, an' amPll warrant yell feel all the better on't."

The sick man looked at her with eyes full of in- tense emotion; doubting, fearing, longing, despair- ing. His fingers moved restlessly upon the quilt, after a fashion that his grandmother, experienced in the death-beds of a couple of generations, had already marked as denoting the near approach of the end.

Oh, Bill, tell us what iffis, and dinna look at me like that? Aw canna bide it, hinny I Thou knows boo fond aw've been o' thee, an' if thou's done wrang an' aw can put it reet, thou may be sartin aw will !"

" Good lass !—Too good for such as me ;" panted Bill, then moved his hand so that it rested on her own, "an' ye've got a lot to forgive me—a lot more than ye think for. Give me a drink—an' raise me a bit—an' aw'll tell thee all aboot it !"
Bell did what he required. She was a born nurse ; strong, capable, and yet gentle in all her movements.

As she moved aside from her seat at the foot of the bed, Bill's gaze wandered to the wall behind her, and a quick, convulsive shudder ran through him. Bell turned, fancying that perhaps someone had entered the room; but no, there was nothing visible save the cutlass and musket of the defunct coastguard, which his widow had hung up there as ornaments, embellished with bows of rusty crape in token of mourning. " It's like a judginent—to have to face them all the time—an' niver be able to forget for is minnet ! What did that prea.chin' chep say, him as Cuddy's friend gans to hear? Aa' canna mind the words— somethin' about our sins follerin' us round, an givin' us no peace, till we washes them clean off wi' the blood o' the Lamb ? Is that it—Bell? or am aw niuddlin' it, like? But hoo coo blood can wash out ianotlier gets ower me! Look here, ma canny sister, div ye thinkt'at every sin can be forgiven to a repentant sinner—every sin—even—even murder ?"

His voice had sunk to a hollow whisper, and his haggard eyes were fixed upon her face; imploring, in an agonised way, some shred of hope. Bell had turned very pale, and at his words she fell upon her knees, and buried her face in the bed- clothes.

"Not—not murder, Bill! Dinna, for the love of heaven, say it wes that !" "Ay, murder! For what else can one call the killin' of a defenceless man? But listen ! If to dream of it by night, an' to think of it by day—to have it sit opposite you at table, an' feel as if every bite ye eat would choke ye—to waken an' find it stannin' by yer pillow, or lyin' (loon by yer side, wiv its cold grey twisted fyece shoved close to yer own—ugh !—if that's not punishment—if that's not hell on earth, aw dinna ken what hell can be like then ?"

"An' for them to bring ma poor broken bones here—here into his varry hoose, where everything minds one of him, an' for her,—his canny wife, with her heart in his grave, as anybody can see, yet doin' her best for me, an' crying over me, as if aw had nowt to answer for—Oh, Bell, it's been bad to bide whiles !" . .
There appeared to be a certain relief to the dying man in pouring out all the agonies of horror and re- morse he had undergone into his sister's reluctant and horror-stricken ears.

" D'ye mind Granny's dream, Bell, that she thowt stood for good fortune ?" he asked, with a momentary flash of his old humour; a flash, which, from its grim incongruity, sounded ghastly to the listener; "it was- nigh beM' fulfilled in a literal way, an' provin' th' aad wife a prophet, again' her will! But thank Heaven for that, anyway—for sparin' me the gallows, aW mean I" Bell had risen to her feet, and withdrawn herself a little, shuddering in every limb. He was her own—her twin-brother, nearest of any living creature; but this terrible revelation seemed to push them asunder, flesh from flesh, heart from heart. She still suffered with his &Mier- ing ; indeed, as she looked at the worn, wasted features and burning hollow eyes she would fain have soothed, and loved, and comforted him, as a mother does her erring and repentant child. If she could have transferred the burden of guilt, how gladly would she have borne it for him, and offered her life as expiation. But alas only the sinner can pay the penalty of the sin. Supreme human love is powerless before the terrible Nemesis of crime. As she stood there towering above him, big, strong, immovable ; with her white lips set in a firm line, and her clear gaze fixed on his poor, miserable tortured face; she seemed like some beautiful but stern incarnation of justice ready to seal his doom.

There were the living to be considered as well as the dying. "You were nob the only one," she said, slowly and with emphasis, "tell me who were concerned in it along wi ye ?" A feverish flush mounted to Bill's thin cheeks, and he plucked at the coverlet.

..... . "Aw canna tell—aw winna tell, so its nee use fashin' yer heid ower that ! There's some 'ats gann tee answer fort, an' if them had been all—but— but there's others, an' them aw canna split on, were it ever so Bell, lass, ye inaunna ask me." "Only one thing more then, an' that aw hey a right to knaw. Was—was—was ma Dick one o' them ?"

The girl's voice sank to a whisper as she brought out this question. In it was expressed the sus- pense and dread of months; during which time the torturing doubt had haunted her by day and by night. She listened breathlessly for a reply. Bill .shook his head.

"No, he was out on't for once! It was while he was away it happened." Bell breathed a sigh of intense relief. "But it wes'nt a planned thing; not that that excuses me, only wor blood was up when he broke in upon us, overheard wor plans, an' aw wes always ready for a bit o' devilry, an'— an' that's all aboot it—all aw'm gannin' to tell, anyway !" . .

r‘ BA ye must tell it te somebody else, Bill! ye maunna die wi' it on yer conscience." "Nay, one's enough, surely !" " What? An' ma poor Dick to be branded m a murderer, an' mebbe hung if they catch him, like ye an' them others hung poor Lanes! Never I Not while I've gettin' a voice in it, aw warrant I*

iaye -no pity for me, thert r "Pity? Oh,Bill, ';na heart is just achin' wi' pity for thee 1" said the girl; melting at once at the weak, pathetic voice; and silting down beside the dying man, she raised his head gently, until it lay upon her bosom, and kissed his forehead tenderly. "But thou sees boo it is, darlin', thou maunna make things warse 1 Thou maunna hey the innocent left te suffer for the guilty." "But no names, Bell! aw winna give no names, mind !" said the weak voice, with resolute deter- mination.

The confession was made to the lieutenant of the cutter, Innes's superior officer; but that gentleman did not manage to shake Bill's vow to conceal the names of those implicated with him in the shameful deed. Some of them had gone down in the Bonny Bess; he would have to stand for the rest.

"All very well, my man, but that leaves us with no one to punish !" remarked the Lieutenant, in a discontented tone, "how do I know this is not n got up thing to clear Daglish ? Am Ito have my best men shot from behind rocks, and hung up for the crows to pick at, without making an example of somebody?' "Aw dinna care" gasped the sufferer feebly, " aw've telled—ye—he's—innocent—an' its yer look out noo if ye hunt him to deith ! Aw'm gannin' te face ma God, dost thoo kna.w that, man? Div ye think aw dour gaun tiv Him wiv a lee i' ma mouth —an' a lee told. to .a clarty gauger, forbye ?" "re better gan now, Mr. Brown," said Bell. quietly. "Ye'll get .nowt 'more out ov him, if ye harry him till the breath's oot ov his body. An' here's his poor wife comin' to say good-bye, for the doctor says he en,ww last abune an hour or so. Come thee ways oot wi' me, an' leave them alone a bit!"

Reluctantly the officer obeyed this command. He recognised, however, the force of Bell's words and saw that the dews,of death were on the sick man's brow; and although of an obstinate he was not of a einel nature. There was. evidently nothing more to be gainea by hArassing Bill during his last moments, and it was only fair to leave him to make his peace--if that were possible—with heaven?

The young wife Ailsie was difficult to deal with. She utterly refused to accept the inevitable, and worried Bell by eontinual appeals for encourage- ment and hope. When Bill turned from her weak complaints and querulous murmurs, to rest on the stronger support given by his sister, Ailsie grew bitterly jealous, and wept like a spoilt child, for- getful of all hint ..her own petty griefs. She adored Bill; but it was amadoration exacting and selfish, asking interest for every iota it gave. Bell had enough to do and to bear during those terrible hours.

When it was all over she became conscious of an intense physical and mental exhaustion, such as her healthy young nature had never before experienced; and when Ailsie had sobbed herself to sleep and lay, with the tears not dry upon her dimpled cheeks, looking pretty and flushed, with even a smile com- ing and going, as she dreamt of the loving boy hus- band, blithe s„md well and gay as ever, Bell felt as though sleep Mid rest and comfort were alike im- possible to her. In all times of abnormal weariness comes that queer state when brain and body cease to obey the will, and to remain quiescent, but become instead intolerably restless and active. He had sinned deeply, but God alone knew how he had suffered for it—was there hope for ;him be- yond the grave? She would have given her own life to be sure of this.

Her darling Bill—how she had loved him. There never was anyone like him in her eyes, though she had often laughed at Granny for saying so. The glint of his eye, the sound of his merry laugh, the funny way he had of telling a story. When they were children together, she was for a long while the bigger and stronger of the two; and she remembered quite plainly carrying him on her back up the hill to the house once, after a long day's hunting of crabs, sea anemones, and star fishes in the pools at Frenchman's Bay. She remembered Cuddy jeering at him and call- ing him "lad-lass" for allowing her to do this; and when he cried at the insinuation, how she consoled him by giving up to him all the prettiest of her sea treasures. And now he lay in that other room with his hands crossed upon his breast, and a look of ineffable peace upon his white face. . . _ .

She had always had to think for him, poor lad! He had the mirth and the comeliness, and she the common-sense. That was all over. He needed nothing more from her. All the wisdom of all the Ages might be his now. He was worlds beyond her.
Yet it was as though a Tart of herself had gone with him. Life without Bill I Ah, there was the sting af it
CHAPTER XXXIX.
A STILL SORROW. It was a long time before Bell recovered the shock her brother's revelation caused her.

It weighed upon her spirits even more heavily than the natural grief resulting from the fact of his death, and the knowledge that one of her objects in life, namely, the watching over and protecting him from the consequences of his own madcap doings, was gone for ever. Moreover, she did not exactly see the course she ought to pursue. For a time the horror and the shame com- pletely,. overwhelmed her, and she could not rise above it.

Dry eyed, and with a face as hard and unemo- tional as though carved in stone, she fulfilled her daily round of duties as methodically and carefully as ever. But' when they were over, and she was free, she would sit motionless and idle, gazing with lack-lustre eyes out over the grey heaving sea or into the fire, for hours together ; a state of apathy very uncommon to one of her energetic disposition. Nobody paid any heed to her, nor did any one understand the intensity of the sorrow which was weighing her to the ground. It is the noisy demonstrative grief that ap- peals to the sympathies, and demands most conso- lation.

Ailsie, who went from one hysterical fit into another, and was ready to enter upon the subject of her bereavement with every fresh visitor, was cited as an instance of wifely devotion and tender heartedness ; while Bell, because she made no fuss, and declined to talk about her sorrow, was set down as cold and unnatural.

If there is one thing more than another that ex- asperates such women as the gossips of Brcamish, it is the being put coldly aside when they proffer this pity, so far removed from sympathy, or parade the curiosity which masquerades so cleverly under the name of interest. Everyone who has lived among this class of people knows ' their ghoulish liking for dwelling upon each detail of a fatal illness, and their insati- able desire to hear all the particulars of it. More especially was this the case in Breamish ; where one of the favourite customs was a particu- larly disagreeable one of sitting over the moribund, and waiting patiently to see the breath go out of his or her body. In fact they " waked " the dying instead of the dead. Moreover, this sort of thing unhappily still pre- vails in several fishing villages upon the north coast; when the doctor in attendance upon a sick person has frequently to turn out of the room a dozen or so of withered and witchlike crones who are greedily watchful of every look and movement on the part of the dying, and who, in their selfish eagerness of curiosity, forget that they are using up the air, and thereby shortening the life of the sufferer. They had been cheated out of this, their time- honoured privilege, by the decision and firmness of Bell ; who was fully determined that her brother's last words should furnish no food for village specu- lation and scandal. Therefore she closed the door against all comers, and allowed no one to see the dying man save his wife and herself. Great was the indignation at this in the village. "Set her up for a proud, self-willed, obstinate, rsaleg Alut I" commented Bessie Carr at the

----------- " Fisherman-8 tiest "to her friends and gossips, . when Bell had taken her by her broad shoulders and gently but firmly turned her out of doors, "an' him oor Ailsie's man, forbye ! Aw've a vary good mind to gan back and kaim her hair for her wi' a three legged styule. An' me 'at had all the bother o' providin' for the weddin' ! If ye had the heart ov a man 'stead ov a moose, ye would gan an' myek her open the door to me I" The latter sentence was addressed to her brother, the father of Bill's wife, who was sitting in the public-house kitchen with a mug of beer before him, and a, pipe in his mouth. -- -- But old Carr only knocked the ashes out of his pipe, and refilled it in a very composed manlier be- fore answering: "She's getten her heid well screwed on her shoulders, yon lass !" he said, approvingly, "she knows what she's aboot when she shuts out a let a clatterin', clashin' aatl wives like ye an' yer Ye mind me o' nowt se much as a flock o' seagals swoopin' doon on a harrin' that still quivers wi' life !" div.p: Councillor H. Ronettrs moves .the adoption, of ' the minutes. Referring to the recommendation that. the Museum be open ton 'Thursdays in addition' to Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays, he said the Committee found that this part of the institution they had charge of was becoming increasingly popular ; and they were anxious, as far as poesible, to :rake it meet the wishes of the public by throwing it open another day in the week. If the experiment succeeded he hoped the time Would come when the Museum would he open probably five days out of the six. (Councillor Shaw Green : Hear hear.) 'As to the other resolution with regard to the daily pap..rs which the Committee proposed, with the Council's sanntioe, to supply in the reading room, the list which the Coavnittee gave met all the reasonable requirements ,of ordinary readers of the papers, and covered every possible shade of politics. ,(hear, hear.) And bethought the Committee had acted very fairly in trying to provide not only for the two regular political parties, but even for nondescript.—(Councillor Fleming: ni-mis)—t.ltP very useful but nondescript and short- lived Liberal, Unionist party. (" Question.") Councillor GREZNING seconded, and the minutes were passed.

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTER.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTER.

In the report of the registrar to this Committee it was stated that the interments for the past five weeks were: —Adults, 79, minors, 68; stillborn and premature, 13; corresponding period last year, adults, 78; minors, 47; stillborn and premature, 9. The receipts for the past four weeks were £129 17e. corresponding period last year, £lO5 10s. 4d. Alderman lisstusoN moved the• adoption. An esti- inablessnd generous Latchford lady, had, he said, pre- sented-the committee with a couple of movable sheds for the purpose of sheltering people who had to go to funerals at the cemetery. These shelters must have cost a considerable sum but she felt so moved at poor people who had to go there having nothing to shelter them from the inclemency of the weather that she very generously wrote to him to say she would present the .two shelters to the Committee on condition that he was not to mention her. name. Consequently he was pre- cluded from telling them who the lady was, but perhaps it would eke out.

Councillor BROWN'S said a clergyman was talking to him the other day about the disgraceful condition of the Church of England Chapel—or whatever von Called it--4n the cemetery. They said the accommodation was not sufficient ; and there was none for any kind ni kneeling (.. No eats.") There were no seats-mforth call- ing such. There was no proper accommodation, either, for persons burying their friends, and he was desired to bring the matter forward to see whether something cot* not be done. Aldermon SUTTON: What about the other chapel then? It is the same, I think. Councillor HUTCHINSON thought the seating in the Church of England chapel was quite sufficient—there were as many seats as the chapel would hold. The Magna thought some of the remarks of Council- lor illitchinson justifiable. He knew what Mro Browne meant to BAI-7—that there was not sufficient space to kneel and they wanted hassocks putting in, as in other churches.
Alderman SUTTON : Kneel on their hats. (A laugh.) - - -

Councillor HILL thought all the chapels were very comfortable, but the Committee might consider as to the seating, if neceisary. Alderman HARRISON expressed astonishment at Coun- cillor Browne's complaints, and maintained that the chapels were in an excellent state of preservation, and had everything conducive to comfort. Councillor Browne : Ask the clergymen. Alderman HARRISON said the Corporation had spent a considerable sum upon the buildings, and nothing could improve them unless they were pulled down anaentarged. If people wanted hassocks and other luxuries,they must re-model the chapel entirely, which was not desirable. Councillor FLEMING : Can't afford it. Alderman HARRISON said they were going at a pace rather in expending money, and they would have to halt in their expenditure,and not spend money unneces- sarily on mere fads, and where there was no real sub- stantial grievance to complain about. The MAYOR suggested a deputation to the Committee on the subject. The minutes were adopted. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE.—A QUESTION OF TENDERS. . . .

This Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. r. Hesketh and Sons for the painting and colour- ing of the Council Chamber and small committee room, according to specification, at £93 135., be accepted. The committee also recommended that the tender of the Warrington Slate Co., for the supply of 60 tons of Bux- ton limestone chippings at Bs. 3d per ton be accepted. Councillor HEATON moved the adoption. He remarked that having received permission at last Council meeting, the Committee had had the decoration of the Council Chamber and the ante-room carried out, anl it was a great improvement, and he did not think it very dear. Dr. CANNELL seconded. . _ _

Councillor BLAMIIIRST asked if any other tender had been asked for. The Committee's resolution appeared to be entirely out of order. The Committee had actually gone and done the work, then asked the Council to sanction it. _

The MAYOR : At last Council meeting you all agreed to permi.sion for the work to go on, and you (to Coun- cillor Blackhurst) were then present ; and the amount of money was told, and you said ay. Councillor BLACKRURST : I maintain that it is entirely out of order. You go and do the wors, and then ask us to endorse it.
The MAYOR: You were here, weren't you? Councillor BLACKHURST : But there was nothing before us.

Councillor FLEMING} : I was not aware of this, and was going to ask the same question as Mr. Blackhurst. The MAYOR: Were you here at the last Council meet. ing ? Councillor FtEssnm : I don't know whether I was here or not. (Laughter.) I think the question might be answered whether there were any more tenders. Councillor fiRATON : No, there were not.

COnrielßOT BROWNE pointed out that there was a reso- lution by the Council that no contract over £2O should be accepted without tenders being advertised for. Councillor•Ftxxxxo : Something wrong about it. The MAYOR: You were here last monthly meeting, and it was read out, and you all said ay. Councillor SRAw-GR.RER : I remember, Mr. Mayor,very well. ' Alderman FRANCOHR said he was not at the last Council meeting, but understood permission was given to the Committee to decorate that chamber and the next room. Ile also thought it would be taken for granted that other pople would be asked to tender. After the admirable manner in which Mr. Fletcher did the entrance hall, if he had not been asked he thought it was very bad treatment. He ought to have had a chance of tendering. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said he knew nothing as be tenders, but he remembered very well the matter coming up at the last Council meeting, and the Mayor expressed a pressing desire that the decorating should be done forthwith, and gave a specific reason why. Alderman Burgess said he was very pleased to hear that reason, and suvested that they should adopt the motion made by the Mayor. Councillor HEATON : I remember voting for it, but do not remember there was one name mentioned.

Councillor BROWNS said he did object to the contract being taken contrary to the resolution. He understood that the gentleman mentioned by the deputy-mayor had, told a person that he could have done the work for considerably less money than £93 13s. and he (Council- lor Browne) thought this ought not to be voted, seeing that the committee had taken upon themselves to act counter to the resolution of the council. Councillor Hum; moved an amendment that the sum of £93 13s. be not allowed for the work. He remarked that he heard no name mentioned at last meeting. The MAYOR: I darcsay you did'nt ; thattyou were not listening. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROISICias thought some explanation was due from the chairman of the committee. There were occasions' he believed, on which it would be impossible to obtain tenders, and he was therefore quite prepared, on certain occasions, to depart from the rule which had been laid down by the Council. He thought that if sue- dent explanation was given by the chairman of the com- mittee the Council would grant the amount asked for.

Councillor Dr. CANNBLL stated that he was opposed to the giving of Corporation work to anyone unless tenders had been advertised for the particular work. On the present occasion the chairman told him that there was no one else in the town who could do the work. Mr. FLEMING : Rubbish.

Alderman &moil remarked that an explanation wa, given by Alderman Chandley to the committee, which was sufficient to justify the committee in giving the work to Messrs. flesketh. They must now pay for the work. _

Councillor HEATON said a tender from Elesketh and Son was Sent in before last Council meeting, and brought before the committee. He objected to any work being let otherwise than through the agency of advertistrr, He was, however, over-ruled on the ground that it waS neceirary to have the work completed immediately, for a special occasion. Councillor ROBERTS expressed his satisfaction with this statement, and hoped that the committee would recog- nise the principle in future for which he had contended. They could not afford to allow the idea to go abroad that any cominittee had done anything in any manner other than a straightforward one. (Hear, bear.) He believed that the contract made in the present instance was done with the best of intentions, and he would not press the matter further. (Hear, hear.) . Alderman HARRISON said he remembered that Alder- man Chandley, who was in the same business, cave it as his opinion at the committee, that the amount was a very reasonable sum. The Committee thus felt re- assured, and having regard to the request of the Mayor that the mem would be wanted for a special purpose in a short time, they at once proceeded with the work. lie hoped the Council would pass the matter over, and, he was sure, in that event, the discussion would not have been in vain. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were adopted. MARKETS COMMUrTEE.
The total income, from all sources, cf this Committee for the past four weeks was £342 15s. 5d.; correspond-

ing period last year, £328 Us. 101. ; increase £l4 3s. 31. T IP minutes were confirmed on the motion of the Mayon, seconded by Councillor BLAmmuncrr: GAS COMMIPTEE.—PROPOdED LARGE EXPEND!.

post of chairman, of the committee. But he believed that Alderman Holmes had thetparadenee of the Coun- cil, and not only of the Council, but of the whole of the town. (Hear, bear.) Councillor DECON : You are quite mistaked. (" Oh, oh.") Alderman FRANCOMB hoped the Council would support the Mayor's ruling in that matter. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor H. ROBERTS said they were bound to sup- port the ruling of the Mayor and he had ruled that the remarks of Councillor Dixon were entirely out of order. Councillor DIXON said he should vote for the amend- mept.—_ _
The Mayort : Take your chair ; take your chair. You are out of order. _ .
Councillor DIXON: That may be so. I quite under- stand that, but it does not alter me. Alderman BURGESS (to the Mayor) : Have !you no power to support your.order ?

The MAYOR : Yes, I think so. Alderman BURGESS : Then tout it in force. Alderman HARRISON : It would be rather disagreeable to do so. Councillor Dam; at this point took his seat. Councillor H. Rol:mars said he most cordially endorsed the remarks which had been made by Alderman Fran- comb with reference to the repeated attacks of a per- sonal nature which were made upon Alderman Holmes. Memners of -the Council might differ from Alderman Hnlines's policy as chairman of the Gas Committee with- out making personal remarks, which were as distasteful to the Council as they were unjustifiable. (Hear,- hear.? 'There was no man in the town who had served it with more disinterested motives than Alderman Holmes had dine: and now, when he had reached such a ripe age, it was the duty of every member of the Council to protect him from insults similar to those to which they had just listened. (Hear, hear.) There was an old saying that necessity made strange bedfellows, and that saying had been exemplified in the case of Councillor Dixon supporting a motion which had been submitted by Alderman Burgess. (Laughter.) In his wildest imaginings he had never hoped to see the lion and lamb—he would not say which was i which—(laughter)—lie down together n the Coun- cil Chamber. (Renewed laughter.) He then sup- ported the amendment of Alderman Burgess. With regard to electric lighting great improvements had beerrniade., aqd they were such that they demanded the consideration of the Gas Committee. He believed the Gas Committee were considering the question, and had taken steps to furnish themselves with the latest possible information upon it, and he hoped that when they' asked for additional borrowing power that they would show that, in addition to what they produced that day, they were not overlooking the possibility of being re- quired to, supply a certain amount of electric lighting. He suggested the withdrawal of the last minute. Alderman HOLMES said that after consulting with Councillor R. T. Fairclough, they had decided to With- draw the minute objected to. (Hear, hear.) Alderman &alum also withdrew his amendment, and the minutes were then agreed to, with the exception of the one relating to the £30,000. WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meeting held on the 4th April, it was resolved that all persons using water for trade or manufacturing purposes be supplied by meter. Alderman Famecomn moved, and Councillor BLACK- ED:MST seconded, the passing of the minutes. Councillor Dam e Are we going to have quarterly accounts monthly ? (Laughter.) I have had two or three sent to my house. No answer was given, and the minutes were agreed to, after which Councillor Dixon left the room.

MARRIAGE OF MISS WILSON-PATTEN. The church of St. Paul's, Knightsbridge, Lrnidon, was the scene on Tuesday of a very pretty wedding, the contracting, parties being Captain the Hon. Osborne Lumley,,llth Hussars, son of the late and brother of the present Earl of Scarbrough, and Miss Constance Wilson-Patten, eldest daughter of the late Captain the Hon. John Eustace Wilson- Fatten and the Marchioness of Headfort House, county Meath,.and grand-daughter of the Right Hon. Lord Winmarleigh, of Winmarleigh,Garstang, Lancashire. A, large number of friends of the bride and bridegroom,, in spite of the very wet weather, assembled at the church, the chancel of which was handsomely decorated with flowers and palms. The bride, who arrived punctually at two o'clock, the time fixed for the ceremony, was accompanied by Marquis of Headfort,by whom she was subsequently given away. She was dressed in a handsome robe of white duchesse satin trimmed with silver embroidery, and a Brussels lace veil fastened to the hair with a diamond bar brooch, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a large bouquet. There were seven bridesmaids, who were very prettily attired in white costumes with green straw hats, trimmed with white flowers. They were Miss Wilson-Patten, Lady Beatrice Paylour (sisters of the bride), Lady Hilda Dundas Lady L. Grosvenor, Miss Paulett, Miss Bridgman, and Miss M. Thynne. They carried very handsome bouquets of white lilac,and were accompanied by a small detachment of men of the 11th Hussars, the bridegroom's regiment. The service was fully choral, the Rev. Arthur Thynne, Canon of Truro, uncle of the bride, and the Rev. Montague Villiers of St. Paul's, Knightsbridge, officiating. The bridegroom was accompanied by his brother, 'the Earl of Scarbrough as best man. After the cere- mony a reception was held at 48, Belgrave-square, S.W. the residence of the bride's mother, the Marchioness of Ffeadfort, when a large and distinguished company I assembled. Amongst those who were invited, most of whom were present, were Prince and Princess Edward of Saxe-Weimar, the Duke and Duchess of Abercorn, the Earl and Countess of Lathown, Lord and Lady Henry Bentinck, Viscount and Viscountess Galway, the Earl and Countess of Arran, Lady Iveogli, Lady Henniker, Lady Stewart, Lord Edward Manners, Sir George Maude, Lady Astley, Lady Lilian Fitzselarance, Lady Edith Drummond, Hon. C. Duncombe, Lady Adeliza Manners, Lady Cantelupe, Lord Molyneux, Lady Scar- borough, Lady Edmond Talbot, Lady Stormont, and the Hon. Miss Murray, Lord and Lady Morris, Hon. A. Fitz- clarence,Lady Constance Leslie, Lord and Lady Zetland, Mr. Wyndham and Lady Grosvenor, the Hon. Mrs. Percy Wyndham, Hon. H. W. Dandas, Mrs. Leigh of Lyme, Hon. Mrs. Rowley, Col. Clayton, Mr. and Mrs. , George Drummond, Col. Alfred Thynne, Gen. the Hon.C. Thesiger and Miss lhesiger,Capt. Matthews,Lady Filmer, Mr. and Mrs. John Thynne, Mrs. and Miss Taylour, Major Shuttleworth, Captain Ridley, Captain Cecil Drummond, and Mr. Charles Thynne. The presents are very numerous and handsome, and 'tame from a very large circle of friends. They included— the Marchioness of Headfort, the bride's mother, a diamond tiara; Lord Winmarleigh, the bride's grand- father, a diamond crescent, and sable trimmings; the Earl of Scarbrough, a diamond brooch • the Marquis cf Headfort, turquoise and diamond bracelet; the Earl and Countess of Zetland, a sapphire and diamond bracelet; the Duke and Duchess of Buceleuch, the Countess of Scarbrough, Duke and Duchess of Abercorn, Countess Grosvenor, Lord and Lady Newport, the Countess of Bradford, the Marquis of Bath, Duke' and Duchess of Leinster, and Dowager Duchess of Buceleuch,' valuable articles. Presents were also sent from the househAd servants at Lord WinmarlEigh4s and the Marquis of Headfort's, the employes at Headfort, Co. , Meath, and the tenants on the Winmarleigh and Scarbrough estates, Sze., &e. Subsequently, the newly-married pair left for Sand- beck Park, near Rotherham, which has been kindly lent by Lord Scarbrough for the honeymoon. The " Star " of Tuesday in referring to the marriage says :—Miss Constance Wilson-Patten who is to be married to Captain the lion. Osbert Lumley at St. Paul's Knightsbridge, this afternoon, is a tall handsome girl of twenty-two, and a great favourite in society. She is the daughter of the Marchioness of fleadford, by her first husband, the late Captain Wilson-Patten, of the Ist Life Guards, and Lord Winmarleigh's eldest son. The bride will inherit the bulk of her grandfather's property, her only brother having died two and a half years ago. Captain Lumley is private secretary and A.D.C. to Lord Zetland, Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and brother te , Lady Zetland, the Countess Grosvenor, Viscountess Newport, and Lady Algitha Orde-Powlett, who are all children of the late Lord Scarborough. Captain Lumley is heir presumptive to his brother—the present Earl of Scarborough. • WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES AND LORD WINMARLEIGH.

The following letter has been received in reply to the resolution passed at a recent meeting at the Conserva- tive Club :—" Wintnarleigh, Garstang, May 2, 1892. My dear sir,—My father begs me to express to you his warm thanks, and to beg you to convey them also, if possible', to all who took part in the resolution passed at the meeting at the Conservative Club, on Thursday, congratulating him on attaining his 90th year, and on the approaching event so interesting to him of his grand-daughter's marriage. He begs me to say how very deeply he feels the kind and hearty feeling shown towards him, and how much he regrets that he cannot, owing to his great weakness, which confines him to his bed, write himself to express his deep appreciation of it. —I remain_, dear sir, yours sincerely, ELLINOR WILSON- PATTEN. H. W. Franeomb, Esq."

The Gas Committee reported that the average illumin- ti fit! power' of the gas for the past four weeks VMS equal to 18 31 candles at both works. The Committee recommended tha adontion of the following resolutions: —That the tender of Messrs.Newton,Chambers,and to erect a two-lift gas holder at Longford, according to specification and plans, at £7,300, be accepted ' • that the tender of Messrs. J. Gibson, to erect smithy and fitting shop, according to specification and plah, at £345, be accepted ; that the tender of Mr. John Taylor, of Garston, to construct gas tank at Longford, accord- ing :to plans and specifications, at £6,500, be accepted; that the Town Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the sum of £30,000 for extensions at Longford Works.

Alderman HOLMES, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that the Council would probably ask why they intended.to make an large an expenditure. When the gasworks were taken over, in 1877, the consumption of gas was 128,000,000 cubic feet. In 1881 the gaaworks were enlarged, as the consumption of gas at that time was about 144,000,000 cubic feet. In 1891-92 the con- sumption of gas was 228,003,000 cubic feet. The pro- duction of gas had thus doubled. The gas made in the year 1891 NVSIS 196.000,000 cubic feet, and the amount sold was 183,000,000 cubic feet. The amount of income for the twelve months ended June 30th, 1878, £33,065, and in 1891 it was £41,795. The return proved conclu- sively that they must extend the gas works; for unless that was done they would be unable to supply the town with sufficient gas. It was proposed to borrow £30,000 for the extension of the gas works. £14,145 would be used immediately, and about £12,000 in the near future for extensions at Longford. The committee thought it would be wise to borrow £30,000 in orddr that they might have a sum in hand to meet expenses which they did not foresee. _ .
Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said that if the commit- tee tatind that it was only necessary t) spend £14,000 of the proposed £30,003, ttyy would only spend that amount.

Alderman HARRISON asked whether the committee had considered the probability or electric lighting making such rapid strides as possibly to diminish the use of gas? Alderman BURGESS thought it a very unusual course to ask for borrowing powers for £30,000 wiren they only required £14,145. No one could tell how, the overplus would be spent. He was afraid the position of Warring- ton in reference to its gas consumption was of a charac- ter which could not be callki satisfactory. The gas works had been purchased more than 15 years ago. Year after year a sum of money had been paid in pur- chase of the annuities; yet after 15 years he believed that he was not wrong when he stated that their indebtedness was as great now as when they took it on. That being the case, he was afraid there was a period of difficulty coming. He was willing that the Gas Corninittee should ask for £14,145, but he would not consent to giving them twice the amount of money they required. He moved as an amendment, that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one referring to permission to borrow £30,000.. Councillor BROWNE seconded the amendment. _

Councillor FrAmmo said that £30,000 was an appall- ing sum to ask for. If the committee had naked for a reasonable amount, he would not have ,objected to granting it. Councillor GREENING supported the proposal of the Committee. . . .

........ Councillor BROWNE was opposed to borrowing so large a sum as that proposed by the Committee, and argued against binding future generations. Councillor Slimy-GREEN said that as the result of the inquiries, he had been led to the conclusion that the committee had acted wisely in bringing forward the re- solution they had done. He pointed out that, with re- gard to the borrowing of the money, the committee woold not expend any of it without the sanction of the Council to every particular item. The extensions were absolutely neeessary. Last winter he believed that fre- quently there was only a twelve hours' supply of gas.

Alderman SUTTON said that in 1878 the production of gas was 128,000.000 cubic feet. The receipts were £33,064. In 1891 the production was 226,000,000 cubic feet, yet the receipts had only increased by about on-fourth. He did not think it was of much consequence whether they applied for £30,000 or £15,000, for in either case they would spend the money as required. Councillor FIEATON said that during last winter there were times when there was only a ten hours' gas supply. He was sure that if the Committee obtained the borrow- inz for £30,000, that amount would not be used without the Council having a voice in the disposal of it. _ .

Councillor TINSLEY considered that when it was pro- posed to spend so large an amount, there ought to be detailed information given. Councillor DIXON supported the amendment, and said that probably there was no establishment which had caused so much dissatisfaction as the Gas Works. ("What about Longford r) Councillor FLEMING: What about Longford? Alderman SuvroN : Longford must be worse, surely. . .

Councillor Dixon, continuing, said that ever since the works had been taken over by the Corporation, six months bad never elapsed without complaints being received relative to the quality of the gas made. Coun- cillor Dixon then proceeded to criticise rather strongly the management of the Gas Works and the Chairman of the Gas Committee. He was a good deal interrupted, and at length the Mayor told him to sit down. He, however, declined to do so, contending that he had as much right to speak as any ther member of the Council. The Mayor then gave several thundering blows on his desk, and at each blow, he told Councillor Dixon, in a loud voice, to sit down. Alderman Faencovin then rose to a point of order, and said that he did not. think any member of the Council should be inaulted in the manner that Alderman Holmes had been.

Coungillor Dixi»; : T say that the public ought not be treathd in the manger they have been--(Cries of " Sit down.") The MAYOB : Sit down. You are out of order. Councillor DIXON : I won't sit down. I have quite as much right to speak as anyone else has. Alderman FRANCOMB said that if Alderman Holmes de- served the strictures which Councillor Dixon had passed upon him, they ought mt to keep re-electing him to the

• LETTER FROM MR. BRUNNER. - In answer to a letter forwarded to Mr. Brunner, M.P., by Mr. Thomas Cooke, secretary of the Life- boat Crew Division of the Runcorn Sons of Temper- ance, asking him to present a petition to the House of Commons in fay our of the Bill for Prohibiting the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors to Children,. Mr. Thomas E. Ellis. M.P., his secretary, writes as follows, under date April 30th :—" Mr. Brunner desires me to acknowledge the receipt of the petition of the Preven- tion of Sale of Intoxicants to Children Bill. He will duly present it to the House. He cordially approves of its pmyer,and will spare no efforts to secure the passage of the Bill."
OTHER PETITIONS.
On Sunday petitions were extensively signed at the churches and citapels,as well as at the Sunday schools, of Runcorn and district, in favour of the Bill.

RUNCORN GUARDIANS PETITION. At the weekly meeting of Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday, Mr. A. R. Norman siad he had expected that the Clerk would have received a communication and petition with regard to the Sale of Intoxicants to Children Bill, but as none had arrived, he wished to pro- pose that the Clerk be authorised to affix the seal of the Board to a petition in favour of the Bill, which was to be read before the Rouse of Commons a second time en May 11th. Mr. Norman drew attention to the very great evils that resulted from selling drink to children, and urged that the Board would only be doing its duty by taking the course he had suggested.—Mr. T. Lea seconded the rantion.—After a brief discussion the motion was carried by a large majority, only three members voting against.
