div.p: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE
ASSOCIATION.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of this Association was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. T. H. Pearson presided, and there was a large attendance of delegates from all parts of tbe divi- sion. Among those present were Messrs. T. W. Legh, M.P., Robt. Pierpoint (Warrington), T. D. Grimke-Drayton, W. H. Brook, W. H. Owen (Rain- bill), C. H. .1".. btorron, 8.. Stuart, B. B. Glover, W. Valiant (Ashton), R. Stone, G. Clarke, A. H. L. Evans, W. If: Gooch, Somers-Cox, Wyndham-Smith, Dr. Handyside, Revs. H. Monk and J. Carson. The Secretary, Mr. W. Mawdsley, read the notice convening the meeting, and the minutes of The last meeting, the latter of which were confirmed. The Chairman was sorry they were prevented from having the presence of several of their friends. In the first place, their President, Lord Gerrard, wrote that he was unable to be present, the reason being that he had to attend to his military duties. Mr. Gillespie was un- well, Messrs. Geo. Comber, J. Ile,ald (Billinge), W. Richardson. W. Jones (tit. Helens), John Hough (War- rington). Alderman Francomb had also sent letters of apology. He was glad to say that the Association con- tinued to prosper to their thorough 'satisfaction. This was now the sixth annual meeting, and they had more inembers now than they ever had. With regard to the local committees, they were greatly indehted to them for what they had done, and as as far as he could see they were now in thorough working order. (Elear,hear.) The re.ult of the last revision was a gain to the party of 109. (Hear, hear.) They had had a large number of meetings in the division ; one which they would remember was addressed by Lord 'Castletown, Mr. Legh, and Colonel Blnndell, at Earles- town, and was a very great success. There had also been other meetings in the division foremost, one at St. Helens, which was also addressed by their member, and he thought it was a very great satisfaction, not only to the borough of St. Helen's but to the county division, that at that meeting there were several gentle- pen who for the first time attended a joint meeting of pnionists. (Hear, hear.) That, he thought. augured ,very favourably for the result of the approaching con- test. (Applause.) Mr. R. Stone (hon. treasurer) said they had again very great pleasure in submitting, what be thought they would consider a very satisfactory statement of the ac- counts of the association, for the last financial year. The expenditure amounted to a little over £3OO, and the subscriptions credited a little over that figure, so that they had a slight profit over the expenditure, and he again thanked them for placing them in the position of having a balance on the right side. (Hear, bear.) The accounts showed that the expenses varied very little over what they had done in past years. The subscrip- tions, he was glad to say, showed an increase, and that, he thought, was a good sign that the association was not on the wane. The accounts had been duly audited by Mr. Voisey and Mr. Barton. The Chairman said that in the few remarks he had. made, he did not refer to one organisation, which he was certain they would agree with him, had been a veryi great benefit to the party in the Newton division, and that was the Primrose League. (Hear, hear.) In cer- tain districts the Primrose League had been a very great advantage. As far as he knew, the prospects for the General Election were never on a more promising foot- ing than at present, and he hoped and believed that their member would be elected by a greater majority than at the last election. He then moved the adoption of the report, which was accepted. ELECTION OF PRESIDENT. The Chairman proposed the reelection of Lord Gerrard as President. He was very sorry they had not had the advantage of his presence very often, but owing to ab- sence from home and other duties he had not been able to• be present so much as he wished. At the same time he thought that they had had a very good substitute, in the work that had been done, in Lady Gerrard. (Hear, hear.) He thought their best thanks were due to Lady Gerrard for the work she had done in the neighbourhood of Ashton. He knew that Lord Gerrard had the most earnest wish for the benefit of the association, and he thought they could not do better than re-elect him. (Applause.)—Mr. W. Valiant (Ashton) seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: AUDITORS, &C.
div.p: AUDITORS, &C.

On the motion of Mr. W. H. 'Owen (Rainhill), seconded by Mr. Wyndham-Smith, Messrs. L. Voisey and R. Barton were re-appointed honorary auditors. On the motion of Mr. Cooper ( Winwick), Mr. Borron and Dr. Handyside were appointed representatives to the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Union of Conservatives.

VOTE OF CONFIDENCE. Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Conservative candidate - for Warrington. said for a number of years now they had honoured him by making him their vice-chairman, and seeing that it was necessary that he should offer himself for re-election to so important a post; they should under- stand, that now he was a candidate for Parliament in another place, there would be a greater demand on his time than there had been hitherto. He then proposed "That this meeting expresses unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and whilst thanking Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., for his services in Parliament, assures him of continued confidence and support at the next election." (Applause.) He trusted when the next general election came about they would return their friend, and his friend, Mr. Legh, not only at the head of the poll, but at the head of the poll by a larger majority than they returned him with at fast election. (Hear, hear.) He understood he was to be opposed by a gentleman who had come from afar, just as he (Mr. Pierpoint) was to be opposed in Warrington, but he apprehended that the gentleman who was oppposing Mr. Legh, would have to take a return ticket, in the same way as the gentle- man who was going to oppose him (Mr. Pierpoint). (Laughter.) In supporting Mr. Legh, they were supporting a very good Government, a government which had done more for this country than any govern- ment, he supposed, in their memory. They had prosperity at home, peace abroad, taxes lightened, the interest on the national debt reduced, a large grant of money which almost freed education for the people, useful legislation concerning mines, trade marks, and many other things, and the navy splendidly strength- ened, not by any haphazard legislation, but by natural reform. (Applause.) The fact was Mr. Gladstone and his friends were striving to get back to power, because they Unsught the electors had forgotten their many blunders from 1880 to 1885, and that the electors were seeking to put them in power' because they promised a great many things, which they knew could never be attempted until the black cloud of Home Rule had been swept from the horizon. (Applause.) Though they , might admire some of the propositions put forward by their opponents, none of ,teill could come Into law. While that black cloud was in the horizon, it must stop the way. While they were supporting Mr. Legh, they were supporting a government that would have nothing to do with Home Rule, a government that was perfectly satisfied with a United Kingdom, and intended to hand it down to posterity one and undivided for ever. ' (Applause.) He prayed them to do all they could to return Mr. Legh, and all the other candidates on their side, and he was sure when they had done so, they , would have done well. (Applause.) i Mr. W. Valiant (Ashton) seconded, and after Mr.l Marshall had supported it, the resolution was unani- mously adopted. Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. said on the four or five previous occasions when he had had the honour of addiessing the Newton Conservative Association, he had congratulated both the members and himself, upon the fact that they bad the field to themselves, in the sense that there was no opponent in the field. To-day they met under altered circumstances, yet he was happy to think that they were prepared to face this new position of affairs with equanimity, if not with confidence. (Applause.) The champion of Liberal principles who had appeared in the constituency was a gentleman of whom he wished to say no ill. Personally he was on very goad terms with him, and there was nothing to be said against him, extept in regard to his political principles. As a candidate he stood in a somewhat peculiar position. He believed he was correct in describing him as an Ulster Protestant Home Ruler, which, if he might use the expression, was a bird of somewhat peculiar plumage. At first sight they might be inclined to ask why, if he was a Home Ruler, he did not stand for a constituency in his own country ; but a very few minutes' reflection would be sufficient to show them that a Protestant Home Ruler was a politician not in much request. They would not have him in the North of Ireland, because they were all Unionists, and they would not have him in the South, because he was a Protestant. (Laughter and applause.) There was no necessity for that division to offer hospit- ality to this wanderer upon the political surface of the earth. (Hear, hear.) They heard a great deal about the importance of the general election, which could not be denied. It was an undisputed fact that it gigantic effort would be made, and every able-bodied voter would be asked to record his vote. He felt very sceptical on this matter. People had been so inundated with pposim during the last 5 or 6 years that they were getting el& of politics altogether. and it would not surprise him if there were not a good many abstentions when the election came round, and if there were many abstentions, he was afraid be must confess they were chiefly to be feared on the Conservative side. ('f No, no.") He was not Speak- ing of that part of the country, but of the Conservative party all over the country. on their side there were a number of politicians whom he must describe as armchair politicians; they did not take an active part themselves, but they found fault with what the Government did. He thought that a man failed in his duty to the country if he failed to take an active part in politics. (Applause.) For what reason, he asked was the Newton division likely to change its member? Mr. Nellie would tell them, if he was re- turned, it was because the electors were panting CO bestow the blessings of Home Rule upon Ireland. He WAS perfectly certain that if a Liberal member was re- turned in that constituency, it would, not be upon the question of Home Rule. The arguments against Home Rule were very much stronger now than ever hefore,ii rid nothing proved that more clearly than the variety pro- gramme, which had been introduced under tlie name of

the Newcastle programme. He had scrutinised that programine to See which fteniln it was most likely to secure support in this part of the world, and he had come to the conclusion that Perhaps the most taking article in it, was the eight hours bill for miners. He had on previ.eis occasions given his reasons at considerable length why he had been unable to support that measure, and he felt bound to admit that some people had found fault with him for this, as an error, in tactics. He thought. it wou,d be admitted that when people were • able to display the united strength that miners were able to display, it would not be necessary to make the aid of Parliament to obtain their wishes. It was Mid that the Unionists were playing tne septennial act against Mr.' Gladstone's life. It woeld be more proper to say that Mr. Gladstone was playing his political life ' against the Newcastle programme, and in doing this Was giving his support to measures which he was not likely to be called upon to carry out. Mr. Gladstone, unfortunately for himself, had fallen into the position of being led, instead of leading. He followed where he thought most votes were likely to be obtained, and he (Mr. Legh) was sure they would agree with him that it was a humiliating spectacle to see such a brilliant man occupying such a position. In conclusion, he said he trusted ha might be able again to count upon their sup- port and assistance. He was not such a fool as to pro- phesy what the exact result of the next election was go- ing to he, but he looked forward to it with confidence. He awaited the result with a certain amount of calmness and confidence ; he felt himself to be inspired and in- spirited by the good cause ; and he felt he had been a ' supporter of a good Government, led by good leaders, and supported by good supporters in that particular division— (Applause.) A. vote of thanks to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. A. L. Evans, seconded by Dr. .Handyside, con- cluded the proceedings.
ANOTHER SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. -` • A SAD CASE.

On ,Tuesday afternoon, an inquest was held by the Deputy-Coronar, Mr. Jones,in the Parade Room' Police Station, iVarrington, concerning the death f of Enoch Monks, aged 32 years,wbo was found dead on the railway at Warrington on Sunday afternoon. Elizabeth Monks, deceased's wife, said she lived at 54, Wilderspool-road. The deceased was a railway labourer, and an army reserve man. She last saw him alive on Friday in Whit, week last year, at home. They were then living at 92, Wilderspool- road, and he was working at Tinsley's tan yard, Latchford. He went out that day, and she thought he had gone to his work, but he did not come back. I She heard from him from Neweastle-on-Tyne, a fortnight after. He had enlisted on the ' day of his leaving home. She did not hear from him again until Christmas. , He was at Ne.wcastle then working for engineers. She had been married to him for two years, and had had one child. The deceased never threatened to take away his life while he lived with her., He told her he had had a, sunstroke. He was always complaining of pains in his' head; and used to fall down.—The Coroner read the following letter which had tre.n found upon the de- ceased r—" 31st April, 1892, Dear wife.—l hope you will forgive me for what I have done, as I am very near out of my mind. I don't know what lam doing half my time. I have done no work since the letter I sent you from the waterworks. I can see very plainly that you do not mean to come. Look after the little one, for God's sake. I have done this to put you free of me. So no more. of your husband— Enoch Monks."- -Edward Appleton, platelayer, employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee, deposed that as he was going home along the railway, on the evening of ths Ist inst. be found the deceased lying across the cabin door, out- side both the rails, at a spot near to Orford Hall. He got assistance, and subsequently went for the nolice,and P.C. Barnett came. The deceased had made a pillow of a handkerchief and other things in the cabin, and the lock of the door was broken off. He had evidently been sleeping in the cabin. There was a small soda water bottle lying about two yards from him.—P.C. Barnett deposed to going, to the spot about 530 p.m., on the Ist inst., and finding the deceased, and upon him the letter just read, some letters from his wife, and some small articles; and the bottle lying on the cabin floor.—Dr. S. Smith said he had made a post mortem examination of the deceased. He found the brain contained more blood than natural, and the liver was very much enlarged. The appearances pointed to death from irritant poison, and indicated oxalic acid rather than any other poison. The doctor smelt the bottle which had been found near the deceased, and which lay on the table, and tasted the remains of a liquid it contained, and pronounced the taste to be that of oxalic acid.—The Coroner expressed the opinion that the deceased had destroyed his life.—A juror said the deceased lodged with him prior to his marriage and he never saw anything wrong in him, and he was surprised to hear about the occurrence.—The jury deliberated privately for a few minutes, and then returned a verdict of suicide during temporary insanity.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. Heaton pre- siged, and there were also present Messrs. Balharry, Davies, A. Jolley, Dobson, Pilling, Shaw, Gill, Hill, A. J. Jolley, Aukland, Fairclough, Clarke, Ratcliffe, W. Houghton, Dignun, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and other officers.

The CLERK said that the auditor, who had lately been at the Workhouse, reported that as far as the Union accounts were concerned the audit had been most satis- factory. He was sorry to say, however, that with regard to the parish of Graippenhall the auditor had had to make a heavy surcharge upon those who had entered into securities for the late assistant overseer. The total amount of the surcharge was Efil Bs.,and he had written to the Ocean Guarantee office with regard to the matter.

div.head: LATE MR. HARBOURNE.
div.p: THE LATE MR. HARBOURNE.

A letter was read trom the Local Government Board, intimating that they had acceded to the request of the Guardians to allow them to make a gratuity of £5O to the widow of Mr. Harbounae, who had been a relieving officer of the Board for many years. A letter was read from Mrs. Harbourne, acknowledging the vote of condo- lence passed by the Guardians, and also thanking the Clerk for the personal efforts he had made with regard to the gratuity of £5O.

div.head: THR HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THR HOUSE COMMITTEE.

The Committee reported that Mr. Ratcliffe had been un- animously re-elected chairman, Mr. S. Davies, .who bad also been cominated for the post, being withdrawn. Mr. Davies was appointed viee-chairman, he having received six votes as compared with four given to Mr. Elibbert, who had also been nominated. A sub-committee had been appointed to examine the yards at the workhouse and report upon what they considered best to be done to improve them. The Master had also been authorised to employ two or three painters to do painting required at the Workhouse.— the minutes were confirmed.
SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee Mr. W. Houghton was appointed chairman and Mr. Davies vice-chairman. The doctor reported that the children kept well.
CONSUMPTION OF LIQUOR AT THE WfiREHOUSII_.

The Clerk said that in response to a request by the Local Government Board a return had been prepared showing the quantity of spirits, wines, and malt liquor consumed in the workhouse, during the year ended 31st, December, 1891.—The cost was as follows—spirits, £2O Os. 3d. ; wine, £ll 9s. 101.; malt liqeor, £8 ss. 7d. The daily average number of inmates in the workhouse during the year was 311. • THE nfATNTENANCE OF LONATTCS. In a return which was read to the Board by Mr. Shearer with regard to the cost of maintenance and removal of lunatics during the year ending March last, it was stated that the total paid was £3,00155. Bd. They received back from relatives £345 6s. 44., from the Count. 7 Council £1,230, from other Unions, &c., EN Bi. 5d., the net cost to the Union being £1,340 10s. lid. During the last six months the medical tees amounted to £26 15s. 6d.; cost of conveyance, £l4 is.; other expenses,such as magistrates' clerk's fees, and relieving officers' expenses, £22 16s. 5d.; total £63 12s. 11d.—Some conversation took place as to the relative cost of keeping the lunatics of the Union under the control of the Guardians and of sending them to the county asylums. The Clerk pointed out that,in any case the Onion would still have to contribute through the rates to the establishment charges of the county asylums He also gave some interesting details as to the scandalou' manner in which a number of lunatics were, many years ago, treated at Newton. The subject then dropped'. e This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: MR. MORLEY ON THE COMING ELECTION.
div.p: MR. MORLEY ON THE COMING ELECTION.

Mr, John Morley was on Wednesday night entertained at dinner at the National Liberal Club, by the London Liberal and Radical members and candidates. Replying to the toast of his health he stated that in his opinion the spirit among English Liberals in regard to the com- ing eleedon was one of undaunted confidence. Their party had never been more ready for the fight. Whene- ever the Liberals had been united they had won. • He hoped they would sink Minor diffarences, and even serious differences, for purposes which were urgent. immediate, and practical. It was uprn rational Radica- lism that they would win the approaching Parliamen- tary election.
Shocking discoveries of wholesale infanticide have been made in Western Russia, sixty-five bodies having been found in one place.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Our neutral contemporary reported Mr. Robert Davies the other day its speaking of holding out the "orange branch"; and explains that it should have been "olive branch." But was the correc- tion really necessary? Was it not a case rather of blundering into the truth ? The Tory party are depending a good deal upon the "Orange branch" in Warrington and everywhere' else.

By-the-bye when is there to be an explanation as to the five questions which the Orangemen of Warrington put to Sir Gilbert Greenall, and have sineo submitted, it is understood, to Mr. Robert Pierpoint ? What are they; and what are the answers of the Tory candidate? The electors, and especially Catholic electors, have a right to know how far Mr. Pierpoint is committed, and whether he has given answers inconsistent with Roman Catholic support.

Lord Randolph Churchill sticks to the word Tory ; and he doesn't see why it should stand in the way of a Liberal Unionist. Nor do we, if the Liberal Unionist depends, as is usually the case, upon being returned by Tory votes. But with the bulk of the Reactionists the word Tory sticks in the throat as " Amen " stuck in the throat of " Macbeth." There was a time when Lord Randolph coupled the word Tory with that of "democrat." How is it now? Has "Tory democrat" ceased to be of value as a political Pry

"An eNst,ryday hero" perished, on Monday, at Parr in the death of Richard Gill, who was injured a year and eight months ago, in King's Pit, Hay- dock, under circumstances detailed in another column. He risked, and, as the sad result shows, sacrificed, his own life in order to save the lives of his fellows ; and, as he did it deliberately, his act was altogether heroic. He held life dear ; but duty was dearer to him still.

Deeming would have done better if he Ii ad not tried to assist his counsel in the plea of insanity. He went on the wrong tack. The wan who is really insane insists rather on his sanity ; so the Rainhill murderer may be said to have tightened the rope round his neck when he set about show- ing that he was not responsible for his actions. He is to be hanged on the 16th May; and, after that, it is to be hoped the public will have some- thing better to think about.

The poet says—" It is not always May," and considering the sort of weather we have had this week nobody need be sorry that it isn't always May. The frost seems to have touched the May day celebrations, for the display in the streets has been remarkably small this year. Time was when there was a Maypole in the Strand but as things go the Maypole may be said to be Strand; even in the country, --- The Gas Committee of the Warrington Corpor- ation came it altogether to strong, in asking for £30,000 when they want to spend £15,000. Suffi- cient for the day are the thousands thereof to be actually spent; and, this being the view of the Council generally, the Committee are requested to "cut and come again." Even if the Council had consented to the borrowing of £30,000, it is very unlikely that the consent of the Local Government Board would have been obtained. It is the rule to require that a good case shall be made out for every penny to be expended ; and a very good rule too. As it is, the indebtedness of Corporations is exceedingly large, and it is rapidly growing.

How was it that nothing was said at the Coun- cil meeting about the Annual Report of the Medical Officer of Health P The report is a most important one, and ought, in the interests of the town, to ho thoroughly considered. A death-rate for the year of 24.63 per 1,000 reveals a grave if not an alarming state of things, seeing that it is 3 per 1,000—that is over 10 per cent—higher than the average of the past 10 years. What about BlacK Spots? Are they being wiped out, or are they growing?

There is to be a Mayoral "At Home" at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening week. Usually the "At Home" is held in the afternoon ; and it is open to anyone to make a call who may think fit to do so ; but in this case special invitations have been issued by his Worship to all notable persons in or connected with the town. Thera is, however, one remarkable exception ; no invitation has been extended to Dr. and Mrs. Houston. This lack of courtesy to the Liberal candidate has excited no little adverse comment, and there is reason to fear that what is regarded as a slight will cause a num- ber of Liberals to decline the invitation. If there is one obligation greater than another to be observed by a Chief Magistrate it is that he should show no political partiality during his year of office. Having invited one candidate to the" At Home," he ought certainly to have invited the other.

The lying spirit which has taken possession of the Tories will continue to operate, it is expected, until they are beaten at the polls. Replying to Dr. Gornall, Mr. Herbert Gladstone deals with Dr. Rentoul's statement as to Mr. Gladstone being "so nearly oft his head," during the Gordon episode, that" they dared not let him see the papers." He characterises the statement as " maliciously false ;" and we don't suppose it will surprise anyone to learn that Dr. Rentoul has previously been under the necessity of publicly apologising for statements made by him which Mr. Herbert Gladstone has shown to be false.

When is the "Warrington Observer" going to follow suit in apologising for its false statements about Dr. and Mrs. Houston? Last Saturday, it published a letter from Mrs. Houston denying the statement that she had sung—" High upon the gallows-tree hung the noble-hearted three"; but there was no applogy to the lady; nor has there been any apology to Dr. Houston for the repeated lie that he was "a Tory in the days of Disraeli," or that equally false statement that he had ordered half a barrel of Warrington beer to be sent to Dublin. Has it come to this—that "the party of gentlemen" has neither morals nor manners?

At the Farewell Reception which was held the other evening at the Conservative Club, Mr. John White entered upon a comparison between Sir Gilbert Greenall and Mr. Gladstone—to the dis- advantage, of course, of the latter. The ex- Premier, statesman, orator, scholar, and author, is, according to the Chairman of the Conservative Party, very small beer compared with the Brewet of Wilderspool. Sir Gilbert's transcendent quali- fication seems to be that he was "born at Wilders- pool ;" and, lest the great fact should be forgotten, why not put it on record as a song for the Primrose League? Thus— It was a Tory meeting, A meeting of " Farewell," When 'Johnny White he up and said— (For so the papers tell) Our Grand Old Man, he's not a fool, For he was born at Wilderspool.

He always was a Tory, And so he always will; Bred in the stupid party, Ile is with that party still; But don't say he's a party tool, For be was born at Wilderspool. It's true that he knows nothing Of the questions of the day; And when he goes to Parliament lie nothing has to say. He goes as goes a child to school; But he was born at Wilderspool.

Althr,ugh he isn't clever, King Beer has brought him " brass ; As for the rest," a-gent " like me Supplies the natural "gas. I don't mind being his footstool ; For he was born at Wilderspool. There now I I've !told you plainly, As plainly as I can— Why, with a smile, we always say Ile i 5" Our Grand Old Man," It's clear as mud, he's not a fool, For he was born at Wilderspool.
ST. EDWARDS .CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN.

It has been the rule for many years to celebrate the first Sunday evening of May in an especially solemn manner. Last Sunday a large congregation attended. The rosary was recited by the Rev. The funeral of thelateMr. Mcwhannell., who was for many years Ship Canal agent at Preston Brook ,took place at Preston Brook on Tuesday afternoon. The funeral was largely attended. The coffin, which was of oak, was covered with wreaths. The ceremony of interrhent was conducted by. the Rev. Mr. Whitley, who was assisted by the Rev. Mr. Clark, curate.

A special session was held at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, for the purpose of hearing an application for a theatrical license to Runcorn Public Hall. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. Henry Reynolds (chairman), Mr. A. Thomas, Mr. James Reynolds, Mr. James Handley, and Dr. Steele. Mr. Salkeld, manager and secretary of the Public Hall, made the application, and Superintendent Atherton said he had no objection. The license was the same that had been granted in former years. MAINTENANCE OF PARENTS IN RUNCORN UN/ON.

Mr.. John Frodshani, collector to the Guardians of Runcorn Union, on Monday, asked the Runcorn magis- trates to make an order upon Wm. Wyche, of London- road, Northwich, to contribute Is. per week towards the support of his "poor and impotent" father, who is in receipt of 3s. per week from the Union. It was stated that the defendant received 235. per week, an had a wife and two children to keep. The requisite order was made.—A similar order was made upon Frederick Gar- ner, bricksetter, of Frodsham, in support of his aged mother. This defendant was in receipt of 30s. a week, and had a family of two children.

DINVER TO WIDNES LOCAL BOARD EMPLOYES.

The advent of the" Merrie Month " has usually been celebrated in Widnes by a procession but on the present occasion this was not to be organised, and it was suggested that the numerous employes of the Local Board should be entertained to dinner. The idea was cordially received by the members of the Board ,who sub- scribed a sufficient sum to succesifully carry it 4fut on a generous scale, and on Saturday evening about seventy of the men employed in the Highway and Health De- partments sat down to an excellent dinner at the Central Hotel. The feast was thomughly enjoyed, and after- wards the evening was spent in singing songs, Src., and Professor Wayman delighted the company by his ventri- quial powers and feats of legerdemain. In the course of the proceedings the toasts of the donors and the host were honoured. The members of the Board present were Messrs. D. Wright, J. Taylor, S. Sadler, and J. Beech.
PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for 50 years,and quality and first-class workmanship are still guaranteed.—Advt.

Mr. George Whiteley, the Tory candidate for the Northwich Division, has a way of turning things topsy-turvy in order to get out of a tight place. If there is one charge which is more clearly proved against the Unionists than another it is that in discussing the Home Rule question, they have tried to stir up strife between the Catholics and the Protestants of Ireland. Mr. Whiteley, of course, knows this, and his idea of meeting the point is to accuse Mr. Brunner of that self-same thing. But the little trick won't work; it can be seen through without spectacles.

The programme gone through was greatly enjoyed by the large audience. MAY DAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. ••_ _ _

In these towns May Day was allowed to by with- out any of that enthusiastic welcome which is the custom in some towns in Lancashire and Cheshire. Many of the horses drawing vehicles of various descrip- tions were gaily bedecked with ribbons, and were a source of attraction to the younger portion of the population.

It is expected that the Markets Csmmittee of Warrington will give ear to the plea of the Shop Assistants' Association in favour of closing the Market earlier on Saturday nights. A public body can afford to set a good example in this respect, and help on the movement for equalising hours. Some tradesmen attach quite as much importance to early closing as to the half-holiday—a point which the members of the Association are doing well to have in mind. At present it may be said to be the key of the situation

They resolved to inform the clerk of the Lancashire County Council that they would be prepared to meet a sub-corn- mittee of that body to deal with the subject of the memorial.

HOLY TRINITY RAGGED SCHOOL, RUNCORN. A. largely-attended concert was held in the Mill-brow Schoolroom, on Wednesday evening, in connection with the Drum and Fife Band, which Miss Evelyn Preston has organized. The Rev. Dr. Preston took the chair. The band acquitted themselves remarkably well. Assistance was rendered by Miss Jones, Miss Simkin, Miss E. Tim- mins, Miss Preston, Messrs. Morris, Rhodes, Hulse, and Scott, Masters F. C. and A. Timmins, and J. Siinkin.

HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The service at this place of worship on Sunday even- ing last was rendered more than usually attractive by the musical portion of the devotions, and there was a numerous attendance of worshippers. Miss Clara Tay- lor gave an effective and charming rendering of the sacred composition "Sacred rest" : and the Mill Brow Sunday School Band performed " Gloria " from Mozart's Twelfth Mass most creditably. Mr. G. S. Frith played the accomPaniments 04 the organ. The preacher was the Rev. F. Withers.

The monthly meeting of this association was held in the Mill-brow Wesleyan Sunday School, on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. A. Norman, who gave a short ad- dress. Afterwards Mrs. Williams and Mrs. Bird,both of Chester, delivered speeches on temperance topics, and referred to the great influence women possessed in do- ing a great work in connection with the temperance movement, Mr. Callis also spoke. During the evening the Halton-road Band of Hope choir gave two selec- tions. Go to PRITCIARD'S for the best Ave guinea watnh a work- ingman can have.-4114. PROPOSHD TRIP TO WORKROOMS CHILDREN. At the fortnightly meeting of Runcorn Board of Guar- dians on Tuesday, Mr. J. Cunnah, the Workhouse Master, was given permission to arrange for the annual seaside trip of the children of the House. Since the trip was organised by Mr. Cunnah three years ago, the young people whose lives are none too bright, have visited Southport, Blackpool, and Llandudno, and in each case the enjoyment of the youngsters has been very great and the effect very beneficial. Mr. Cunnah is dependent upon subscribers for defraying the cost of the excursion, and will gladly acknowledge any contribution from those desirous of rendering aid in carrying out so worthy a project. JOSRPR PRITCIARD IS prepared to wind and keop Ii repair private clocks from 10e. per annum.—Adre. A WOULD-BE DEEMING AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at. the Widnes Petty Sessions, Francis Gaynor' Ellison-st., was again brought up on remand, charged with doing grievous bodily harm to his wife, on the 2nd April, by kicking and beating her.—Mary Ann' Gaynor said she had been married to prisoner about twelve months. On the evening of the 2nd April, he came home and asked her for some tobacco and told her to get his dinner ready. She told him she had not any tobacco. He then used foul language to her, and told her that if she was not gone before he came back it would be another Rainhill case. She went into a neighbour's house, but he found her out, and again com- menced to abuse her. She had a baby in her arms at the time, and he struck it on the head. He afterwards caught her by the hair of the head and knocked her head against the wall, and kicked her several times in the back. She had been very ill since, and for several days her life was despaired of. Prisoner had done sc srcely any work for the past twelve months.—Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

Mr. George Whiteley, the Conservative candidate of Northwich Division, was the principal speaker at a public meeting at Halton, last evening week. The electors, he said, would have to decide a momentous question at the coming election. It seemed to be the policy of Mr. Brunner to stir up religious strife. In the few speeches their member had placed before the elec- tors, there was a distinct desire to stir up strife between one class and another in the United Kingdom, and he ventured to say, that it had not only been his aim and desire, but that of the Gladstonian party to encourage division, strife, and rancour between all conditions of men. Alluding to the temperance question, Mr. White- ley said it would be a mistake to abolish all licenses. He (Mr. Whiteley) did not go in for any great scheme of compensation, but he said if licenses were done away with, those people who had invested their money in the trade, with legislation as it was, had a fair claim for just consideration. (Applause.) The chair was occu- pied by Sir Richard Brookes. The attendance was only moderate. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PAITCHLARD.OI.-411V5.

div.head: Amman ASSAULT BY A. WIDNES SCHOOLMASTER.
div.p: Amman ASSAULT BY A. WIDNES SCHOOLMASTER.

Before Mr. George Pilkington and Mr. Stapleton. Bretherton at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Thomas Shoman, of Birchfield-road, head master at Simms Cross Board School was summoned for assaulting a boy named Arthur Pinnington, aged 12 years, of Albert-st. Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. It was alleged that on the 26th April the boy went to school half an hour late, in com- pany with two other boys. The defendant sent the latter lads to their seats, but, it was alleged, he told Pinnington to remain where he was, got a short cane, and hit the boy ten times with the stick, holding him meanwhile with his head between his (defendant's) knees. He afterwards told the lad to go to his place, Pinnington replying " Yes, and you'll get place this afternoon." Defendant then took him to a private room and on going in knocked him down against the door. W hen in the room he again hit the lad with the stick, and one of the assistants then came into the room with a larger cane, which the defendant also used, striking complainant about the back and legs, which were black and blue and blistered. For the defence Mr. Swift admitted that the complainant had received a tolerably severe thrashing, but that it was no more tbau he deserved, #nd it was necessary in order that the disci- pline of the school might be maintained. The boy it was said had sworn at the defendant. The bench, after some consultation in private, returned into court, and the chairman said that they considered the defendant ' had exceeded his duty, but under great provocation. The justice of the case, they thought, would be met by payment of the costs, amounting to £2 Os. 6d.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO. Mn. F. POPE, OF RUNCORN,
div.p: PRESENTATION TO. Mn. F. POPE, OF RUNCORN,

An interesting gathering took place in Mill Brow Wesleyan Sunday School on Tuesday evening. The occasion was the presentation of a handsome oak writing cabinet, splendidly finished and fitted up with every convenience, to Mr. Frank Pope, eldest son of Mr. S. Pope, who on Thursday left these shores for America in the steamship Cephalonia. Mr. Pope has for some time filled the position of chemist at the Camden Works of the United Alkali Company, and he has gone to the United States with the expectation of securing a lucerative and important appointment there. Mr. J. R. Frith made the presentation on behalf of the teachers and scholars, and remarked that Mr. Pope had been cradled in the Sunday School. His father and mother had both been teachers, while his father had filled every office in connection with the school, and was now one of the superintendents. Mr. Tope had followed in the footsteps of his par- ents, and had been secretary of the school. Mr. Frith then presented the cabinet, which bore the following inscription' on a plate :—" Presented to Mr. Frank Pope, by Mill Brew Wesleyan Sunday School, Runcorn, on the occasion of his resigning his office of secretary,consequent on leaving England. May, 1892." —Mr. Findlow and Mr. Yates also spoke in terms of eulogy of the character and ability of Mr. Pope.—ln a few heartfelt words, Mr. Pope acknowledged the gift, and the proceedings terminated. The Rev. W. Arrow- smith prt-sided. On Wednesday afternoon the workmen of the Camden Works made a presentation to Mr. Frank Pope, of a handsomely fitted-up dressing case. Mr. Flolford vresided, and said that the men had unanim- ously determined to show their esteem and respect for Mr. Pope, by banding to him a slight token, as a reminder of the only place at which he had worked in England.—Mr. Thomas Badge, the oldest employe, made the presentation, and spoke of the effiaient way in which the recipient had performed his duties as one of the foremen at the works.—Mr. Pope thanked the men for their kindness to him.

div.head: POACHING AT HALTON.
div.p: POACHING AT HALTON.

Four Ship Canal labourers named Davis Byrne, Samuel Worthington, John William Povah, and Arthur Clarke, were summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of trespas- sing in pursuit of game, on land at Halton, in the occupation of John Henry Houghton. The defen- dants pleaded guilty, and William Knight, one of the gamekeepers to Sir Richard Brooke, having described how the defendants attempted to dig rabbits up and sent their two dogs to chase hares, each was tined 10s. and costs Bs. 6d. A WARRINGTON MINSTREL TROL7PE AT WIDNES. On Monday evening the Warrington White Star Minstrel Troupe journeyed to Widnes, and gave an entertainment in St. Patrick's Schools. There was a large attendance, the chair being occupied by Mr. H. Wade Deacon. The troupe, which is compara- tively young as yet, acquitted themselves in an ad- mirable manner, and the merriment which was kept up throughout the evening, fully showed that their efforts were appreciated. A special word of praise is due to Messrs. Coggins and Newton, come- dians, who contributed very largely towards the success of the entertainment. Mr. George Riley ably acted as accompanist. On Tuesday, before Mr. W. I. Thompson, an old woman named Mary Giblin, of Pendlebury-lane, Sutton, and Bridget Mannion, her daughter, were charged with stealing a gold and diamond ring, value 505., from the residence of the Rev. W. R. Parry, Congregational minister, Robin's-lane. Pri- soners were arrested by Police-constable Fillingham and when charged Mrs. Giblin said she took the ring from the backyard window sill, thinking there was no harm. She put it on her finger, and on the following day her daughter saw it and took it from her. The daughter admitted this, and said she put it on her own linger, and went into a neighbour's, where Joe Cropper took it off her and put it on his wife's finger.—The Chief Constable asked for a re- mand, which was granted.—Prisoners. on Wednes- day, admitted taking the ring, hut did not think it any good.—They were both tined 10s. or seven days.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. THE NEW RAILWAY FOR Sr. HELENS.

In consequence of the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Company not being able to come to terms with the United Alkali Company, Limited, in respect of land required by them in the township of Windle and Parr, an arbitration was arranged under the Railway and Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1875. The railway company possess powers to construct a line from Lowton to Liverpool, and will go through the townships named. The route fired upon necessitates the ac- quisition of about two acrea of lam: belonging to the Alkali Company, and £lO,OOO is claimed. The railway valuers put the total at £3,000, the chief dispute being as to the bleaching chambers at the Globe Works. The court sat in private on Thurs- day, with Mr. A. Sinclair for the Alkali Company, and Mr. E. Doming, of Manchesterfor the Railway Company as arbitrators.

THE FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FARMER AT HIGH LEIGH. The inquest on the body of Mr. Richard Whitlow, farmer, High Leigh, who was killed by being thrown out of his trap on Wednesday night, last week, was held on Monday, at High Leigh. It will be remem- bered that the deceased gentleman was raturning home from Warrington, late on the night in ques- tion, and when at the corner of Swinyard-lane, High Leib. he ran over a heap of stories. The result was - that the trap was overturned, and the horse was thrown to the ground. Mt. Whitlow was subse- quently discovered under the trap, and when he was extricated it Was found that he was unconscious. Tne injured man was conveyed home, where he lingered until seven o'clock on the following morn- ing. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

CHESHIRE LINES WORKMEN'S PROVIDENT SOCIETY.

The 17th annual meeting of the Cheshire Lines Platelayers' and Workmen's Provident Society, which consists of the workmen employed in the engineer's department of the Cheshire Lines Rail- way, was held on Wednesday, at the works, Batters- by-lane, Warrington. In the unavoidable absence of the engineer, Mr. W. G. Scott, M. Inst. CE., the chair was taken by Mr. W. Corker, Permanent-way Inspector, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and delegates from Lancashire and Ches- hire. The Secretary submitted the annual report, which stated that the number of members was 989. A large amount has been expended in aid of the 29-1 sick members who had received assistance from the funds of the society, and 24 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed, Mr. Thomas Pratt, was re- elected secretary for the ensuing year, and Messrs. G. Walker and W. Hughes were elected auditors. The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman, officers, and others.

UNION Caunctc—On Sunday sermons were preached in the Union Church, Frodsham, by the Rev. James Irving, London. The collections amounted to £l7 165., and were in aid of the chapel funds.

FRNE CHURCH.—A service of song, entitled "The Ministry of Jesus," was given in the Free Church, Frod- sham, on Sunday evening, when there was a fair attend- ance. The songs and solos were nicely rendered by the choir. The narrative was read by the Rev. R. Trotter. CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT FRODSHAII.—Mr. Henry Tollemache, M.P.. addressed a meeting of his supporters in Frodsham Town Hall on Monday evening. The Chair- man (Mr. J. Reynolds, J.P.) moved a resalution of con- fidence in the Government and it was seconded by Mr. Dawson, and supported by Mr. Tollemache, who said during the eleven yearshe had represented the division he had done what he believed to be best for the country, and he had given a steady but not a slavish support to the Government in its conduct of affairs. That Mr. Brundrit's description of the scenes that occur in Greenway-road on Sunday eyenings, waft a faithful picture, and his warning and the action of the police ought to have the effect of quelling the boisterous spirits, whose horseplay was the cause of much annoyance and discomfort.

That a movement is on foot to form a Temper- ance Federation in Runcorn. In these days of unions of one description and another, why should not the temperance societies of the town federate to carry on more effectively the good work they are doing? Mr. T. Cooke has charge of the affair.

That the Runcorn Commissionetrs practically without discussion declined by the casting vote of the Chairman to allow the seal of the Board to be attached to a petition in favour of the Children's Liquor Bill, not ostensibly because they disagreed with the Bill, but because they are so extremely jealous cf giving the weight of their influence in a manner in which the act which formed them did not contemplate.
That it is a pity they are not always so anxious to keep within the letter of the law.

That the appeal of the Runcorn Technical In- structinn Committee has been issued, and let us hope that it will not be disregarded. The litho- graph of the proposed Institute, which forms the frontispiece ot the appeal, is capitally executed and well worth preserving.

PROPOSED STOCKTON HEATH SEWERAGE. - With regard to this matter, the Clerk read a reply from Mr. Percival Silcock that he would forego his charges for the work that he had already done (drawing plans, &c.), on condition that the proposed scheme should be committed into his hands to carry out in which case his charge would be the usual one of five per cent, on the cost of the works. —lt was resolved to ask Mr, Silcock if his charge of five per cent, would include supervision.

div.head: SEWERAGE OF HELSBY : A SHOCKING PICTURE.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE OF HELSBY : A SHOCKING PICTURE.

The Local Government Board forwarded a letter from Mr. F. B. Mason, solicitor, Chester, enclosing one from Mr. Frederick Thorniley, of if eLsby, with regard to the sewerage of that township: Mr. Thorniley in this letter, which comprised 32 folios, said the sewage of Helsby passed into ditches, these being used for watering mulch cattle, which had no other water to drink. The drain, age of the township was undoubtedly in a very defective and primitive state, and totally inadequate. The sewage was almost absolutely carried by open ditches or sewers, and eventually passed into the Manchester Ship Canal. All these open ditches gave off a very offen- sive smell and were most detrimental to health.— Mr. Thorniley requested that a Local Government Board Inspector be sent to Helsby to make inquiry.—Mr. Brandreth said the Committee appointed to deal with the matter, were not alone to blame. When Mr. Farring- ton was prepared to do something, Mr. Thorniley had objected to him going on his land.—Mr. Brandreth con- tended that it was no use carrying out an extensive sewerage scheme unless there was an efficient water supply because the pipes wculd only get silted up with sand from the hill. Mr. Brandreth said Mr. Thorniley turned his own private drain on to Um railway, and created a "regular stink " on his own place, and he ought to be made to abate the nuisance. He suggested that the letter should be sent to the overseers of Helsby, who should be requested to call a ratepayers' meeting to consider the question. The Clerk read a report of the Helsby Committee submitted in December last, in which they state that the drainage of Helsby would compare favourably with other places situate in the same sanitary district in which extensive sewerage schemes had been carried out, but if the sewer on Mr. Thoreiley's property were diverted from the pre- sent course it would be a great improvement. This alteration would have to be made with the consent of Mr. Thorniley and the iiint railway companies.—Mr. Farrington said he had ascertained from the assistant engineer of the railway companies that there would not be the slightest chanee of them agreeing to that diver- sion consequently he thought it was no use approaching Mr. Thorniley.—Mr. Farrington said he would see what could be done ; and the Clerk was instructed to inform the Local Goverment Board, that the matter was having attention.

div.head: BILL CLIFFS BURIAL GROUND.
div.p: BILL CLIFFS BURIAL GROUND.

I Mr. Farring7;;LlCl-Veitii respect to the outbreak of fever at Hill Cliffe, he had inspected the cottage, and had ordered the sanitary arrangements to be improved as far as possible. Be was of opinion that the insanitary state of the property was not the sole cause of the out- breaks of fe4er. After heavy rains he had seen offensive matter oozing out of Hill Cliffe grave yard, which was 1 eight or nine. feet above the road, and in his opinion the crowded state of this burial ground had something to do with the outbreaks. He thought interments should lac stopped in the old burial groand.—Dr. Adams con- sidered there were too many buried there.—Mr. Baxter expressed doubt as to the grave-yard causing the disease. —Dr. Adams said his report last meeting properly ex- plained the outbreak as due only to the abominable sani- tation of the cottages.—Mr. Farrington was instructed to make further inquiries with regard to the burial ground.

• sorrow WATER SUPPLY. The Local Committee deputed to deal with this ques- tion, reported that they had appointed a deputation to wait upon the landowner, and ascertain what amount he would contribute towards the cost of obtaining a supply.—lt was resolved to engage Messrs. Timmins, engineers, of Runcorn, to test the probable yielding capacity of the mill. THE WATER SUPPLY OF STOCKTON HEATH. Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, Warrington, wrote with respect to the Stockton Heath Sewerage Committee that he had not time to devote to the committee His pre- vious letter was written about water more than sewers. He was apprehensive of the future supply at Stockton Heath. Mr. Ross, the secretary of Warrington Water Works Company, told him that he feared there would be no supply if many new houses were built at Stockton Heath. Mr. Logan Wright had bored to a great depth —l3O feet—without success, and he (Mr. Davies) doubted if there was any water left in the stra,um. There was no doubt that the cause of these wells being dry was the Ship Canal, and he felt certain that the water wold never crmae back even when the Ship Canal was finished. If it did, lie feared it would be sea water or worse. What was really wanted was water towers in Stockten Heath, and he ventured to suggest an interview with Mr. Ross on the subject. which he should be glad to support if required.—The Clerk was instructed to coin- municate with Mr. Ross on the subject.

div.head: LYM M.
div.p: LYM M.

LYMM VOLUNTEE —The Lymm Volunteers held a RS. parade at the Drill Hall, on Saturday, the band attend- ing. On Sunday the Volunteers marched to Oughtring- ton, attended divine service, and afterwards returned to headquarters, where they were dismissed. Lymn Local. BOARD.—Thei monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, On Tuesday evening. There were present—Messrs. Hugh Harrison, F. Swal- low, Richard IVhitelegge, John Perrin, James Holt, Alex. Mclntyre, Samuel Appleton, T. J. Ridgway (law clerk), and William Mallard (clerk).—Mr. Underwood, in a long letter to the Board, complained of a nuisance which Mr. Smith, his neighbour, was causing. He stated that if the Board could not rectify the matter, he should have to apply to the Local Government Board. The Surveyor was ordered to call upon Mr. Smith, and ask him to abate the nuisance at once.—From the Gas Manager's monthly report it appeared that there was a decrease of 5,000 -cubic feet of gas compared with this period last year. div.head: TURNING SUNDAY INTO PANDEMONIUM
div.p: TURNING SUNDAY INTO PANDEMONIUM
ItIIIICORN.

On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, six res- pectably-dressed youths named Charles Cook, Thos. Barrow, David Coventry, Frank Stretton, William Miller, and Alfred Gregory, were summoned for having on Sunday evening, the 24th April, unlaw- fully obstructed the footpath in Greenway-road, by loitering thereon to the interruption of passengers travelling thereon.—P.C. Crowder said the defendants and about eight others were standing on the footpath that runs alongside the Cemetery. They completely blocked the footpath, and he noticed about a dozen people who had to leave the footpath in consequence. Because of the great crowd that assembled, he and P.C. Worth could not take the names of more than the de- fendants.—P.C. Worth corroborated, and said the de- fendants were singing to each other.—The defendants stated that they were about to bid good night to each I other, when the constable came up. They denied that they were singing or making any noise whatever, or ' that they had been previously warned.—Mr. Brundrit said that they had done a very good thing in bringing forward this case, for there was no doubt that very dis- graceful scenes took place in Greenway-road on Sunday nights. He had never seen them, but living so close to he had frequently heard them. There were youths going about in droves, and it was positively not fit for any young, woman to go past some of them, ips they would either pull her about or make some rude remark. It was quite time this kind of conduct was put a stop to. Some of the defendants had been warned before, but this would be the last warning they would get, and if they were ever brought there again, and he were presid- ing he would make an example of them. Each defendant was ined Is. and costs 10s. 6d. Mr. Brundrit gave the defendants another warning, and said the conduct that went on in Greenway-road made it more like Pandemon- ium than Sunday.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. SAMUEL TAYLOR.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. SAMUEL TAYLOR.

The mortal remains of Mr. Samuel Taylor, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, who died on Wednesday at the advanced age of 80 years were committed to their last resting place on Saturday afternoon. A hearse from the establishment of Messrs. Yarwood, Bros., conveyed the body to the Cemetery, where it was carried into the chapel and thence to the grave on the shoulders of Messrs. D. Bisbrown, John Green, Philip Matthews and John Ramsden. The mourners were the Rev. James Taylor and Mr. Edward Taylor (sons) the Rev. Henry Lewis (son- in-law), Miss Lillie Taylor, Miss Nellie Taylor and Miss Alice Taylor (granddaughters). The deceased gentleman had been intimately connected with the Wesleyan Society for sixty years and the following members of that body paid their last respects to the dead :—S. Pope, C. Littler, R. Norman, T. Simister, D. H. Jones, S. Coventry, Joseph Bazley, James Gregory, Captain Davies, Jabez Unsworth, Thomas Boote, S. Ravenscroft, Arnold Unswortli, James Higgins, William Kay, Jeffrey's, T. Molyneaux, J. R. Frith, S. C. Beckett, John Lunt, John Stubbs, Thomas Rushton,E. Ince.—The service in the chapel was conducted by the Revs. H. Lewis, James Hanley, and Thomas Wilkes and at the grave side by the Rev. Thomas Wilkes and the Rev. W. Arrowsmith.—Mr. Thomas Bradshaw was the under- taker.

I On Sunday morning, at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, the Rev. T. Wilkes made a brief reference to the death of Mr. Taylor. As the result of some little in- quiry, he had ascertained that the departed received the first note of entering the society 60 years since last Dec.,and remained a member to the date of his death. In 1841 he was appointed a leader,and had been over since. He began with one member, but for many years he had , a large class, the members of which testified to the good work he performed. For along period he was a Sunday school teacher, and during the most part of his life, he was remarkable as a sick visitor. The preacher was informed that he did a great deal of acceptable work in the homes of the poor and among the members, whom he visited when unwell. He was a constant attendant at the means of grace, Sunday and week days, and frequently took part in prayer meetings, lie was told that for 25 years after his conversion Mr. Taylor never missed a single love-feast, and not many even during the last 35 years, and at them he always bore testimony. His moral character was blameless. An intense love for tie Master and faith in Christ dominated him in his feebleness, and he died as he lived—a faithful Christian, and he (Mr. Wilkes) had not the slightest doubt Mr. Taylor was that morning among the white-robed throng befoterGod's throne. He believed the deceased was a true Methodist and a true Christian, who served God according to the light he had ; and now he rested in peace. Might God's blessing be given to the bereaved ones.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night, Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, (vice-chairman), Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Handley, S. Taylor, and George Moss, (clerk).

NEWTON SCHOOL accommonermx. With regard to the want of school accommodation in Newton district, the Clerk stated the Committee ap- pointed to deal with the matter had held a meeting, and it was intimated to them that there was an intention to enlarge the Shaw-st. school. No recommendation was therefore made to the Board.

div.head: SPECIAL I'EES QUESTION.
div.p: THE SPECIAL I'EES QUESTION.

The Clerk reported that he had forwarded the follow- ing letter :—" Aptil 6th, 1892, Rev. Dr. Preston. Sir,-1 am directed by my Board to draw the attention of the managers of Holy Trinity Schools to the special scale of fees which is at these schools applicable to children who attend very regularly, and I am to inform you that the parents of these children when appearing before the Board protest their inability or unwillingness to pay the extra fees required of them. In such cases the Board does not feel itself justified in taking proceedings to compel attendance in view of the obstacle existing at the schools ;indeed it is doubtful whether the magistrates would grant a conviction under such circumstances. I am therefore to ask if your managing committee will be • good enough to consider the difficulty alluded to, and see if they cannot discontinue charging these extra fees in order that there may be no obstacle in the way of the Boald carrying cut its compulsory powers with respect to the children in question."—ln reply Dr. Preston states that ten years ago the question of the persistent irregu- larity of children attending thesc schools was carefully considered by the managers.and with a view of remedy- ing the evil it was decided that in all cases of gross irregularity an extra fee be demanded. This arrangement had worked very satisfrctorily. In the absence of any direct statement to the contrary, they felt justifiad in maintaining that they had acted within their rights and also in the interests of the chil- dren attending their schools. The amount received from irregular scholars as extra fees amounts to about £2 per annum. The managers had now resolved to discontinue the practice of charging extra fees, relying for the future upon tha Attendance Com- mittee to deal with the irregular scholars.—The Chairman said as they bad decided to cease charging extra fees the reply might be considered a satisfactory one.—Mr. Handley said when they found that it was not in their power to charge fees, they dropped them.—Dr. DcDuugall : I think they have complete power to charge extra fees.—The Clerk read a letter received from the Education Department on 3rd March,lBBs, in which they invite the managers of Hely Trinity School to rescind the resolution under which the practice of charging double fees was in force, so that one of the obstacles the Board had encountered in discharging their statutory duties might be removed—Mr. Handley : It is clear enough that the Education Department do not approve of it —Mr. McDougall : They invite the managers to rescind the resolution, but it does not say that they are doing an illegal act.—Dr. Gastaldi : The question is they ought to have rescinded the resolution eight years age and they never had.—After some further conversation, the clerk was instructed to enter the letter on the minutes.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The School Attendance Committee's minutes con- tained the report of the school visitors, from winch it appeared there was an increase in the attendance for the past month, as compared with the corresponding month last year. The number on the rolls was 3.605 ; last year 3,640. The average attendance was 2,937, against 2,795, and the percentage 82.8 against 81-3.

A TENNIS eIIIB. On the proposal of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Taylor, it was decided to allow the teachers at, Green- way-road School the use of the schoolyard for the pur- poses of a tennis club.

IF:OMM OF SALEM On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, the salary of Mr. T. Green, assistant master at Greenway-road School. was advanced to £55, accor- ding to the scale of the Board.

WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB. On Saturday afternoon 21 members of the above club, with several unattached riders, bad an enjoy- able run to Cranage, the weather being beautifully fine. On Monday there was a fair turn-out of mem- bers who rode to Knutriford to witness the May- day festivities, both outs being greatly enjoyed. On Thursday evening the members of tile club held a smoking concert at their headquarters,the Norton Arms hotel, when a pleasant evening was spent. . _

div.head: CASE FOR THE CROW
div.p: THE CASE FOR THE CROW

When Mr. Deakin had concluded his address to the jury, Mr. Walsh addresied thecourt for the Crown. Ile gave a dispassionate review of the evidence of the different witnesses, and claimed for the prosecution that they had brought home the guilt of the murder to the accused by a chain of evidence in which not a 'single link was missing. The defence, on the other hand, had not only left the main issue untouched, but had utterly failed to prove that the prisoner, at the time of the mur- der, was in such a condition of mind as not to be respon- sible for his, actions. STATEMENT BY THE PRISONER. . .
When Mr. Walsh sat down, Deeming, acting in opposi- tion to the strongly-expressed advice of his counsel, asked leave to make a statement to the court.

The judge at once gave his consent, and Deeming then made a long, rambling statement of an irrelevant kind. He declared that whatever the verdict might be he would feel that he had not had a fair trial. He asked for justice, not for himself, but in the interests of the public in general. It was not 'the law which had dealt with the case, but the Press had prejudged it. The photograph published in the news- papers gave the first clue by which he was identified. He had been most unjuStly treated. There were, he as- serted, not two. hundred people in Melbourne who would not lynch him to-morrow without any trial if they got the charece. If he had been guilty he would much rather have said so than be for four days in court an object of scorn to the ugliest rice of people on the face of the earth;,who grinned at him fromthe galleries, and shook their fists at him. He accused the witnesses Woods and Hirschfeldt of lying. The evidence of Flirsch- feldt was, he said. a gross instance of treachery. Many of the Crown witnesses he had never seen before. He complained that the trial had been forced on so that there was no chance of evidence being got from Eng- laad or Calcutta as to his mental condition. He had borne the trial patiently, and had never in terfered, but nobody had watched the case closer- His nights had been devoted to reviewing the evi- dence and making notes. His memory was defective ; he would lose it suddenly for months, and then regain it for several months continuously. He felt in his own mind that he was not guilty. He had no reason for killing his wife, who was kind and affectionate. He be- lieved that if there was proper cause for committing such a crime it was justifiable, and that no law should inter- fere. He, however, had no cause. He had one comfort ha the knowledge that she was not dead. He did not say that to screen himself. He thought no more of life than of a piece of 'paper ; his life was ruined even if he were acquitted, and he should commit suicide in the Yarra. He had travelled over the whole world. On the Zambesi he had been attacked by savages and knocked on the head. On one occasion he entered a den of lions, and dragged one out and gava it to a Mr. Jones, a Liver- pool man. Having run such risks, he attached rib value to life. He complained of the treatment which he had received from Dr. Shields, the prison doctor, and declared that it was a disgrace to himself and his fellow-creatures. It was not possible for the judge and jury to give a fair verdict, and whatever the result, he would consider that he had not had a fair trial. He was alone and friendless, and every man' a hand was against him. Even. Miss Rounsevell had been turned against him. He proceeded to deal withthe main features of the evidence, and then suddenly said •—•"-I cannot remember the proceedings of the court, tha witnesses, or the evidence." Throughout these remarks the prisoner spoke boldly. and fluently, though there was an occasional tremor iri- ' his voice. Resuming his address he finishedlup by declaring he knew where his wife, whom he was sup- posed to have murdered, was now living. He would not, however, disclose her whereabouts, because of her terrible crime. As soon as the accused had stopped speaking, The Judge commenced to address the jury, the sum- ming up being a lucid and impartial review of the evidence, and of, the law as to insanity in cases of murder. . • THE VIIRDICT AND SENTENCE. The jury their retired to consider their verdict, and returned into court after an absence of just an hour, Amid breathless silence, the foreman announced that they found the prisoner guilty. In response to the usual inquiry as to whether he had anything to say why sentence should not be passed upon him., 'The prisoner declared that he was innocent of the murder. 13,e had not had a fair trial, and a postpone- ment had been refused him because of the expense. He- was careless about the verdict, as if he had been azquit- ted he Should have committed suicide. The jury had been influenced by the press. He was not at all dis- turbed because the•world thought him guilty, but he longed that Miss Rounsevell should be convinced of his 'innocence. In conclusion, he asked the judge not to make any speech in passing sentence upon him. Whether influenced by this request or not, Judge Hodges merely pronounced the formal death sentence. Prisoner, who walked boldly out of court with, his hands in his pockets, was then removed to the cells below prior to being placed in the condemned cell.

- - THE DATE OF THE EXECUTION. lliltur,nounwn, TUESDAY .—On his return to gaol from court yesterday evening, Deeming was ordered to be put in prison attire, and was placed in the condemned men's cell. In, order to prevent any attempt at suicide prisoner was put into irons. Deeming's manner was then quite cheerful, and he passed a calm nightoleeping peacefully. On waking this morning he resumed writ- ing his biography. It is expected that the execution will take place on the 13th inst.

BREAKDOWN OF THE PRISONER: MELBOURNI., WEDNi.SDAY.—The utmost pneeautions are being taken to prevent Deeming from coratnitting suicide. His demeanour since yesterday has visibly changed. This morning he in completely broken down. At intervals he bemoans his fate in a piteous manner, declaring his innocence, and upbraiding, his solicitor. He has asked Mr. Lyle to assist him in making his will, and has declared his intention of leaving what little be has to Miss Rounsvell. He Still declares his intenticm to kill himself before the date of the execution, if he gets a chance.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT OF A RAZOR.

At the Borough Police Court, on -Thursday morning, Thomas Godfrey and Michael Fearney, militiamen, stationed at Orford Barracks, were charged with steal- ing there the previous afternoon, a razor, the property of James Parry, or with receiving it knowing it to have been stolen. A colour-sergeant and Private Wiliams de- posed to Godfrey taking the case containing the razor from between the mattrass and the bed in a bed- room, and handing it through the window to Fearney. On being accused of the theft, he denied having the razor, but ultimately produced it from his sock.—God- frey was lined 10s. including costs, and Fearney ss.

div.head: CHARGE OF STEALING A DOG.
div.p: CHARGE OF STEALING A DOG.

David Bramhall. plasterer, 66, Sharpe-st.,was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, with stealing, on Saturday night, a dog which had been chained up in the yard of the Bull's Dead Inn, Church- at., kept by John Evans. The Chief Constable said Mr. Evans was satisfied that the prisoner had been persuaded by some other men to take the dog, and did not mean to keep it. The prisoner he (Mr. Hunt) believed was on his way to return the dog, but foolishly called at the General Wolfe, where some men recognised it, when one of them striking it, it ran back to the inn. Mr. Evans, who did not appear, wished to withdraw the case. He was absent through having been called to London.—The case was allowed to be withdrawn.

div.head: THEFT OF CLOTH.--A COOL CHARACTER.
div.p: THEFT OF CLOTH.--A COOL CHARACTER.

_ At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, John Connor. of Liverpool, but last from Manchester, was brought up on .remand, charged with stealing, on the morning of the 3rd inst, five pieces of cloth, value £5, the property of Messrs. Bovdell, woollen drapers, Bridge-st.—The Chief Constable said since the prisoner's remand he had been recognised as a man who was COM- mitted from that Court to Liverpool, where he was sentenced to five years' penal servitude, for stealing boots, in December, 1886. He had been in jail a time or two since serving the five years.—Henry Beddell, assistant to the prosecutors, deposed that a boy told him of the theft, and he ran after the prisoner, and took the cloth from him, and was bringing him laack when he met P.C. Corbett and gave him into custody.—P.C. Corbett said the prisoner admitted the theft.—The pri- soner's Only answer to the charge was that the cloth was unravelled; if it had been in rolls he would have got away with it.—The Chief Constable: You would have carried it better you mean 2—The prisoner :That's it.— He was committed for trial.—The prisoner, who Is about 45 years of age, has passed about 20 years in prison.

div.head: ALLEGED EI7RGLART.
div.p: ALLEGED EI7RGLART.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, William Beesley was charged with burglariously breaking into the premises of Thomas Hesketh,3,Wilson-, Patten-st., on the 20th April, and stealing a bevel plane,, T square, awl, brush, bottle of whisky, and a pocket knife ; secondly, with entering the same premises on the 11th March, and stealing two pictures and a magni- fying glass; and thirdly, with stealing from the Museum, on the 22nd March, a coat, the property of George Knott, the porter.—The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) appeared for the prosecution .—Thomas Hesketh stated that during February he moved from Grappenhall to his present residence in Wilson-Patten- st. The prisoner helped him to do so. On the 19th April he was working in the cellar, and was using the joiner's tools now produced. After' he had finished work he made the cellar grate safe, and went away. On the next day he found the grate unfastened and tlae tools I gone.—Mary Leslie, wife of Wm. Leslie, pawnbroker, 1 Mersey-street, said that on the 20th April the pri- soner offered the joiner's tools for pawn. She gave him a shilling for them.—The second charge was then pro- I ceeded with.—Mr. Hesketh said the magnifying glass I and pictures were his property. He valued the pictures I at £7.—Catherine Gibbon, pawnbroker, deposed to pri- soner coming into the shop and offering the articles for 2s. 6d. She gave him that sum after he had stated that they were his property.—George Knott, porter at the Museum, stated that the coat was his property. On the 22nd March he took off his coat whilst he did some work. , Returning to the room where he had left it shortly after- wards, he found the coat was missing. There were four i keys n the pocket.—George Wilson, in the employ of Mr. Jackson, pawnbroker, Church-st., said the prisoner Pawned the coat there for 2s. 6d. On being charged with the offence by Detective-Sergeant Monaghan the prisoner replied, "That coat belongs to me • I bought It for 3s. 6d."—Beesley now pleaded not guilty to each of the charges, and was committed to the Assizes for trial.
