div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.-RUGBY,

What the value of a successful Cup tie means is shown by the Cleckheaton balance-sheet. The result of their victory over Leeds Parish Church was a £l5O gate at home against Bradford, and the debnit of £lOO standing in the ledger against the club at the beginning of the season was transferred to a credit balance of £l2.

It appears that the Brother James, the Swansea half- backs, only had a brief stay in Hartlepool, and the rumour has it that they have returned to their "ancient mountains." It is perhaps as well that they have done so, although West Hartlepool P.C. would doubtless have liked them to have stayed on in County Durham.

Wigan wound up their season in brilliant style on Saturday by defeating the powerful Runcorn team on the latter's ground by two tries to nil. It is the first time during the winter that the "myrtle greens " of Runcorn have been taken down at home. Wigan dur- ing the season have played 40 matches, won 23, lost 11, and drawn 6.

• There was a fine crowd at Lancaster on Saturday to see the champions of the North-Western Rugby Football League (Millom) in active opposition to a team selected from the rest of the clubs. The season just closed has shown in a remarkable manner how beneficial League competitions are for both clubs and players, and the present status of the clubs within the jurisdiction of the League is owing in a material manner to the interest which has been taken in the matches.

Millom have earned their position by consistent good play. Apart from the distinction which the title of champions confers on a club, Milloin become the holders of an exceedingly handsome silver cup, presented to the League by the Mayor of Lancaster.

div.head: ASSOCIATION:
div.p: ASSOCIATION:

The junior teams of Warrington have had a fairly she- cessful season. The Penketh Friends' school shows up well with 13 wins, eight losses, and one game drawn, 127 goals being scored on their behalf against 74. The Warrington Association have won 11 games, lost 13,and drawn 3, their opponents notching 49 goals to 39. The Warrington Rangers played 28 ' matches, winning 14, losing 13, their total score being 149 points to 101.

The game of football, under both codes of rules, came to a definite close on Saturday, so far as England is concerned. The season has been a very eventful one, chiefly noticeable for the fact that the ruling bodies have exerted a stronger and firmer hand over the players they control, with the result that brutal or unfair play has certainly become a decreasing quantity. Despite the exaggerated "butcher's bills," which have appeared from time to time in London papers, the existence of which depends on the daily supply of exaggerated and sensa- tional statements, the game has never been so well or scientifically played as in the campaign which concluded on Saturday. •

The Lancashire Football Association can look back upon a satisfactory season. They began with a balance of something like £76.0, and will be in the same position when everything is squared up. The Junior competi- tion has done better than ever, the semi-final and final ties yielding a total of £282, whilst the three "semis " and the final for the Senior Cup have produced £B5l. The Rovers will get the best haul out of the competition, as they figured in two semi-finals and the frnal, so that although they did not win the Cup they will do well financially.

The four clubs wile reached the English 'semi-finals have a fairly good haul this year owing to Notts Forest and West Bromwich Albion being so considerably gener- ous as to play three matches. The only hardship to my mind is that Aston Villa and Sunderland get just as much out of the proceeds as the two clubs who were the means of procuring the gates ; but that is the rule, and last year Sunderland had to play Notts twice. Sunderland and Notts Forest each receive £166 16s. 91, while the Albion and the Villa get double as a reward for reaching the final. £323 is a fair addition to .the exchequer, and the Albion can very well do with it, for their alleged supporters do not bestow too much money on one of the most plucky teams that has ever carried off the English Cup.

CRICKET. On Wednesday W. Chatterton was made much of at Derby. and presented with a cheque value £l6O by Sir Henry Wilmot, V.C., who highly complimented the pop- ular Derbyshire cricketer on his extraadinary success at the Cane. Chatterton has played with the Derbyshire team something like nine years, and although often tempted, he has remained true to the county ot his birth.

M /SCE LLA NEOIIB. A gymnastic competition, which was open to com- petitors from clubs in all parts of the kingdom, tosk place at the Liverpool Gymnasium, Myrtle-st., on Satur- day afternoon. In the strength and agility competition, D. Templeton, Liverpool Gymnasium, scored 221- points, D. Walsh, of the Warrington Gymnasium, running him very closely with a score of 21 points. Prizps were afterwards presented by thp Bishop of Liverpool and other gentlemen.

Five persons were seriously hurt on Wednesday by the fall o f s. bridge at Bramley Station, near Leeds. The extensive flour mill stores of Mr. George Body, Gladstone-st., Cardiff, were on Wednesday morning en- tirely destroyed by fire. Mr. Gerald Portal, British Consul-General. has re- turned to Zanzibar, on the successful conclusion of his expedition to Lamm and Witu. The town of Lamu made absolute submission to the British agent. and the Flnglish flag has been hoisted in all the tosvna of Witu- land.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
TRANNERE WANDHRERS V. WIDNES.—Played at Birken- head Park on Saturday. Result—Widnes 1 goal and 1 try ; Tranmere Wanderers 2 tries and 4 minors.

RUNCORN V. WIGAN.-At Runcorn on Saturday. The visitors immediately broke away, Halliwell scoring twice. The game was fast and interesting, but at the interval Wigan were leading by two tries. The second half was stubbornly contested ,each side in turn pressing. Neither scored, however. and Runcorn were defeated on their own ground for the first time this season by 2 tries to nil: WARRINGTON V. KENDAL HORNETS.

The season 1891-92 was brought to a close on Saturday, and judging from the attendance, and the enthusiasm which was displayed at Wilderspool when the return match with the Hornets was brought to an issue, the public were loth at being compelled to make way for the summer pastime. The weather favoured the latter sport, and there would be close on 4,600 present at the time of Ricking off. It was refreshing to see Barnes, the once popular centre, turn out to do !duty, this time officiating at wing, though it was to be regretted that he should meet with an accident in the last few minutes, it being ascertained afterwards that he had broken one of his ribs.

Wilson kicked off, and soon Warrington were at their opponents' goal, the attack being brought about by James and John Bate and Jolley. Beard and Allen relieved slightly, and, Boscaw only partially replying, Ahen was awarded a mark, but little or no ground was made by the venture. Jolley spoiled Robinson, the Ulverston threequarter, and Warrington were attacking their opponents' goal in ding-dong fashion. Allen again was the saviour of his side, and intercepting a pass to Heesom, ran clean into Warrington territory before he was pulled up. Thorntley and Holmes dribbled effktively, and from a scrimmage at half way Barnes effected a brilliant run to the Kendal line, his pass being poorly manipu- lated. Some loose play followed here, and then the Warrington half barks passed neatly, and James Bate, running strongly at the finish' finished up the effort with a try between the posts, Barnes placing a goal. The kick-off saw play at IVarrington quarters, but Donohue, Ashton, and Buckley with an excellent rush soon had the ball at its original end. Ashton ably led his men in one fine rush; and when within a couple of yards of the posts, made a vigorous effort to get in, but found the host of Hornets too much for him. Robinson and Whiteley cleared the danger temporarily, and Ash- ton tried to make his mark, but failing in the attempt, he and Donohue took the oval to the line by neat pass- ing, and Handles wound up the sequence by scoring near the corner flag. No sooner had the drop out been effected than a surprise came from the foot of Boscisw, for some fluctuating play was taking place at Kendal quarters, and Beard kicked wildly to the home custo- dian, who took the chance proffered, and for the second time the Kendal goal was lowered, the feat being hailed with cheers. Warrington still aggressed, their passing if anything having improved, and the Hornets' defence was feeble indeed. Beard and Allen raised a hope, but the effort was a spasmodic affair, and passing by Barnes, Heesom, and the Bates neutralized the advantage gained. James Bate got away from centre and ran through the thick of his opponents, Barnes just failing to take the final pass. From the scrimmage near the line, the county half back received from his companion half, and feigning to pass in his progress he again got in. this time Ashton failing with the place Ashton and Turner each experienced hard lines, but amends were made the next minute, for the home backs treated the onlookers to a bit of exchanging, and after the halves had done their share, Heesom and Barnes tried their skill, with the result that the old hand outwitted his opponents, and scored between the posts, John Bate placing the goal. Heesom Thorniley, Donohue, and Jolley maintained the attack,, but the Kendal men played up pluckily, and got dangerously near the home lines, Fisher dribbling well. Donohue came away from the thick, and this latter effort being seconded by Barnes and Daniels, play was on the visitors' lines when the interval arrived with the score—Warrington, 3-2-1 ; Kendal Hornets, 0-0-1. On resuming, play for a while was of a give-and-take order, and only of an ordinary description. Eventually, passing byJolley,Ashton, Thorwiley, and Donohue forced the oval at the Kendal goal, the home skipper step. ping into touch a yard from the line. The Kendal men next had a chance, and some amusement was caused when Lally (a Warringtonian) brought Turner down, and a wild pass saw the oval being taken over, and Jackson scoring under the posts. Allen's kick was charged down by Fair Turner. Jolley and Heesom were effective in their tackling, but a neat run by Lally and pass to Robinson again saw Boscow saving. Barnes and the Bates again passed well, and the former essayed a futile shot at goal. Robinson meeting the kick, and compelling a third minor to be conceded. From this the Hornets bad shot their bolt for a fine run by Holmes ended in his passing to Bandies, and the last point of the season was scored, Turner making a good attempt at the place. Soon after Barnes was obliging with one of his old-timed runs when he met with the accident referred to above. Nothing of moment occurred after this, and the final score read— Warrington-3-3-4; Kendal Hornets, 0-1-3. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back; Daniels, Me- son, and Barnes, three-quarter backs ; James Bate and John Bate, half-backs, Ashton, Turner, Ra,ndles, Jolley, Buckley, Donohue, Thorniley, Molyneaux, and Holmes, forwards. Kendal Hornets : Whiteley, back : Allen, Robinson and Hesmondelgh, three-quarter backs.; Leaks, and Beard, half hacks ; Moores, Houghton, Wil- son, Fisher, Jack.on, Weightman, Sun, Harrison, and Lally, forwards.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE.

-- A house in Borthwick-road, Stratford, Essex, was the scene of a distressing tragedy, on Wednesday morning. Thomas Dickson, a clerk, and his little girl, aged one year and ten months, were found—tho latter on the bed, and the former on the floor—with their throats cut. It appears that the deceased man sent his wife- out about ten o'clock, and when she returned she found her husband and child lying with their throats cut. Infor- mation was at once given to the police, who state that there is no doubt that the affair is a case of murder and suicide. The deceased man, it is understood, has- for some time been in a depressed condition.

May sth, 1892.

It was discovered on Wednesday morning that during a heavy gale which prevailed in the night a number of boats had been swamped off Bangor. Considerable damage was done at Preston. A telegram from Holmwood, Edenbridge, to the Press Association, says Lord Bramwell'a condition continues very grave.

div.head: YEAR 1892.
div.p: THE YEAR 1892.

We take the following from "The Hundred Year Al- manac," a European publication held in the highest repute for very many years all over the Continent on occount of its almost marvellous gift of correctly pre- dicting the coming seasons., and what may be expected to accompany them

" Venus will be the evening star for the year 1892. The year will be a more moist than dry one. A beautiful and late spring will be followed by a warm, sultry, summer, which will produce lots of good grass and grain. EARLESTOWN v. LE/OW—The cricket season was opened at Earlestown on Saturday afternoon, in favour- able weather, when Earlestown and Leigh opposed each other. Much interest was centred in this match 'from the double fact that Earlestown would for the first time put the abilities of Miller, their professional, to the test, and that Leigh would becaptained by the famous county player, D. P. Lancashire. Both players gave excellent accounts of themselves, and fully justified the interest that had been taken in their performances. Miller, however, was hardly up to form, being some- what indisposed, but his score of 33 showed that he was not in any sense a novice with the willow. There was a great crowd to witness the opening fixture, aid as the game progressed the excitement reached fever pitch, which was intersified when it was found that Earlestown had managed to secure victory by the small . maprity of two runs. .Score.:— _

DEEMING' TRIAL & SENTENCE.

Mxt.notrasia, MONDAY.—The interesting evidence given by the doctors on Saturday has tended to. increase if possible the interest in the Deeming trial, and the Criminal Court was through the morning, besieged by ' an immense number of people. The first witness called for the defence was Mr. Davison Symons, the reporter who travelled with the , prisoner after his arrest from Perth to Melbourne. Ile 'billy described Deeming's alleged fit in the train, which he said was a very violent attack. , Dr. Springthorpe, who was next c-alled, repeated the evidence he gave before the opening ef the trial, when a postponement of the proceedings wac,being considered. Dr. Springthorpe was pressed to give an opinion, as to the prisoner's responsileility for his actions, or his ability to commit the murder while in an epileptic condition, but declined to commit hitnsAf without further material ,upon which to base a decision. Dr. Pishbourne said all the prisoner's symptoms, both mental and physical, pointed to brain disease. The case for the defence then closed, and the mut adjourned' for lunch.

SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF-HOLIDAY.

Sir,—This question has now been before the public for some eight or ten weeks, and I (along with othcr tradesmen) am greatly pleased and gratified that on April 28th so many of the tradesmen of Warrington had the manliness to commence to close their shops again, after the trying ordeal of two weeks' cessation. This alone is sufficient in itself to cause the weak-minded tradesman to give way ; but what do we find ? Why, sir, instead of a great falling off in the number of those who close their shops, we find a great accession in num- bers of those tradesmen who are willing to give the half-holiday, and who have adapted themselves to cir- cumstances. There are a few black sneer, in every fold, and so we find a few mighty ones who say in effect they will not concede a half-holiday whether the public favour it or not. I earnestly trust that the public of Warrington will take note of the attitude of the few tradesmen who are trying to frustrate the half-holiday for Warrington shop assistants. The more this question is considered the greater the desideratum in its favour. I hope that every tradesman who has commenced to put up his shutters at one on Thursdays will never be influenced by those who try to break up this well-nigh established half-holiday. I will not argue the pros and cons of the question. That has been done. I think that our leading townspeople are only waiting to see what the tradesmen are doing for themselves, and that tradesman who has the largest heart shall receive the largest syrnoathy.—Yours, Sze„ A TRADESMAN. Warrington, 29th April, 1892.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON. Sir,—The death knell of the present Parliament has been sounded ; its demise may take place any day, and the question is, when buried, who or what is to be its auccessor ? Shall a legislation of "Shreds and patches" again hold the reins of power, and patronage? Or shall we return to Parliament men who will give us whole measures—instead of delusive enactments like County Councils without control of police, or drink traffic, or sanitary authority ? The County Councils are simply road-menders and scavengers. They may have done a good deal in a small way, but county control they have little or none. The Act is a 191ank cheque, and wants filling up. We have had an Allotments Ac', and are to have a Small Holdings Act, but neither one nor the other has a bottom in it. The electoral laws are an anomaly : they may suit the rich and well-to-do, but to a very large portion of the people they are an injustice, an annoyance, .a delusion, and a sham. These, and a hundred other hardships under which the people labour, require redress, which can never be got from a Tory Government, and can only be had by the people sending to Parliament enlightened, liberal,and just-minded men. I care not whether they are of the working or wealthy class, but there must be intelligence,—political intelli- gence—and sound statesmanship. The gentleman who has come forward as the Liberal candidate for Warrington seems possessed of these quali- ties in an eminent degree,and his meetings, his speeches, and his statements on the various burning questions of the time, have aroused a feeling of enthusiasm among the masses seldom exceeded. Shall that enthusiastic feelini, die or become either cold or lukewarm ? I hope not. 'There is no building in Warrington sufficiently spacious to hold the people who would attend a good Radical gathering. Then let us meet in the open air under the canopy of heaven. Allow me, sir, to interpret a Welsh quotation—" In the face of the sun, in the eye of the light, the truth against the world." It was sug- gested in the Co-operative Flail, at Dr. Houston's last meeting, that we should meet in the open air on Satur- day afternoons, and why not? There are many who would come to an open air meeting who would not care to enter a building. Let us by all means lay hold of all we can ;we may convert some and confirm others. No means should be neglected in educating the people in political knowledge, dispelling the delusions under which I many labour from the teachings and misrepresentations of Tory Lords and Primrose Dames. Any man who knows anything of the past political history of this I country must know which of the two parties has given him most political power,most social power and influence, which has made knowledge and scientific attainment the most easy of access, and done the most to elevate his condition socially, morally, and intellectually. The Liberal party need not fear the scrutiny, and will come forth from the ordeal with high honour. Let us then keep pegging away. When Dr. Houston is not here, let us show that we have not forgotton him, or the advice he gave us to work as though the election can oxly be won by the individual effort of each good man. I am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. Sankey Bridges, April 26th, 1892.

div.head: WHY TORIES OPPOSE LABOUR REFORMS.
div.p: WHY TORIES OPPOSE LABOUR REFORMS.
81r,—The other night I listened to Mr. R. Pierpoint's speech, which was utt=rly void of all promise to attempt
to amend a single unjust law which is now destroying

, the trade of the Empire ; although he was requested to answer such questions as the Amendment Bills of Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties, Employers' Liability Bill, &c., which the Trades Union Congress, in September last unanimously carried, " expressing its strong dissat- isfaction with the Government for not giving facilities for its consideration," and urging upon the various societies and Trades Councils to make "a test question at the next general eLction." They had it recorded that during the past year there had been 383 cases tried, and in only 109 of these had compensation been paid, and that only to the amount of £8,047, 14s. ed. "The law charges in connection with these were (held to be) greatly over the total amount paid in compensation. This being so, the law, as at present, was a fallacy, and a fraud on the working classes." Mr. R. Pierpoint, as a lawyer, knows why he shirked

answering such questions as these. He said much in his speech about "swallowing anything." So with the Tories and a few thoughtless Tory working-men dupes: " notwithstanding the pain and nausea," as Mr. Pier- point gulled them, "they were prepared to swallow any- thing" ; hundreds of millions of pounds to compensate such Tories, brewers, and publicans which " the Gruid Old Sheik," voted for. Although he utterly neglected other duties in Parliament, he was wide-mouthed enough to swallow anything. Tory lawyers want to go to St."Stephen,sto serve their own ends. Working-men are to be needlessly maimed and killed by explosions, in mines, ceffin ships on sea, Sm., while lawyers of the Pierpoint Tory class are receiving fees for prevent- ing the amendment of the Acts referred to, and more than all, the sums obtained by widows and fatherless children under the Emphyers' Liability Act of 1880. Yet such Tory lawyers as Mr. Pierpoint and Dr. Rentoul are so delighted with the true interest of working- men, care so much about them and whether thee are killed ! Rather are they filled with Tory greed or La. d. and such lawyers' fees that there is nothing left for the working-man's family to buy the common comforts of life with, and they are so engrossed with the present decline of trade that when the vital questions i concerning the sad state thereof are put in writing, or n. pubhe meeting, to their lasting shame be it said Mr. Pie!-point refused to give a reply, while ha unblushingly claims to be fit to deal with the destinies of the Empire. Dr. Rentoul talked and talked pothouse bosh, and empty twaddle, and his glib tongue betrayed his heart- less lack of statesman-like concern and knowledge of trade matters. He said " As to milling royalties, I Ilan; not studied them and know nothing about them. Wise M.P. to come to Warrington to pose as the champ- ion of Tory working-men ! Yet such "fory M.P's , and advocates, who did not make a single promise con- „cerning labour questions, or the worldng-man's rights ,to have a voice or vote in amending unjust laws, or „making laws in St. Stephen's, are just the right kivicl for the file cutters of the Trades Council ,who objected to allow the Trades Union Congress tabour test questions to be dealt with as they ought. , ! that they and all other poor oppressed working- men would think more about the vital labour law reform so urgently required at present, and vote only

for those on whom the nation's weal devolves! And as the book of books says : " Behold the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth : and the cries of them that have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. ' And He has moved upon the hearts of such high moral men as Mr. W. E. Gladstone, to be His instruments to effect a change for the better in Eng- land as well as poor oppressed Ireland. oye ! whose hearts God has touched, do your duty! Be wise, ye ministers of Christ, ye teachers in the Sabbath School, ye working and merchant men. Your votes, given on the wrong side, can only lead the empire nearer the verge of ruin. Such tnen as Sir Gilbert Greenall and Mr. Robert Pierpoint are opposed to Sunday Closing of public-houses, local option, and true Land Reform. Then vote at the next General Election for such men as Dr. Houston, who will work for all such vital reforms.—Faithfully yours, A WORKING-MAN. Warrington.—April 29th, 1892.

THE BUDGET DEBATE: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN LIBERAL AND TORY FINANCE. Sir,—ln view of the discussion on the Budget, I beg to draw your attention to the great increase in Taxation under the present Government. Although, by calling certain taxation " Local " which was previously classed as " Imperial," a nominal reduction of Imperial Taxa- tion has been effected, yet the burden upon the taxpayer has been increased, including these, i.e., putting the figures of Revenue in the same form as they were put previous to Mr.Goschen's accession to office, the amounts raised in taxation each year are as follows :
PUBLIC REVENTID.
GL tDSTONE GOVERNMENT.
SALISBURY GOVERNMENT.

1881, 31,872,354 1887, 90,772,758 1882, 83,955,229 1888, 89,802,254 1883, 87,386,505 1989, 89,883,332 1884, 86,160,184 1890, 94,563,137 1885, 87,988,110 1891, 96,562,988 1886, 89,581,301 1892, 98,593,000 So that, so far from having reduced taxation, Mr. Goschen has increased it from £90,772,758 in 1887, to £98,593,000 in 1892_ Despite this fact, the fixed charge for the reduction of the National Debt has been reduced from £28,000,000 to £25,000,000, the following being the amounts :

div.head: NATIONAL DEBT SERVICES.
div.p: NATIONAL DEBT SERVICES.

GLADSTONE GOVERNMENT. SALISBURY GOVERNMENT. 1881, 29,575,264 1887, 27,958,023 1882, 29,665,945 1888, 26,213,911 1833, 29,679,093 1339, 26,224,594 1884, 29,651,526 1890, 25,226,760 1885, 28,548,239 1891, 25,207,000 1886, 23,449,678 1892, 25,200,000 171,569,750 156,030,288 So that, notwithstanding bad trade and war, the Glad- stone Government devoted out of taxes 15i millions more than the present Government has done, and though, thanks to chance surpluses, the present Government may have absolutely reduced the National Debt by a larger amount than their predecessors, they have not reduced it to anything like the extent they should have done con- sidering that the amount paid for interest alone in 1887 was 2,4 millions less than the amount paid in 1881, thus allowing a larger portion of the fixed charge to go to repayment of capital ; and that the rate of interest has been lowered. _ . . _ . .

The chief causes of the increased Taxation have been the extra grants towards the relief of real property from Local Taxation (made at a time when the popular demand was not for the reduction but the increase of Taxation on Land Values), and to the increase in the Naval and Military Expenditure, the following being the figures : - ------------

„ . . We have deducted from the Gladstonian years the amount of grant to India towards the cost of the Afghan War, and added t 9 the Salisbury period the amounts spent out of loans. This Government has in a time of peace expended eighteen minims more than their prede- cessors, though the latter had to carry on an expensive war and prepare for threatened hostilities with Russia. The Financial Policy of the present Government may be summed up as follows. They have in time of good trade : (1.) Increased the amount of taxation from £90,772, 759 in 1887 to £98,539,000 in 1892. (2.) They have reduced the amount set aside for pay- ment of interest on and repayment of capital of the National Debt from £23,000,000 to £25,000,000. (3.) They have thereby set aside for National Debt purposes out of the Annual Expenditure during the past six years £158,030,288, as against £171,569,750 fcr the preceding six years, or 15i millions less. (4.) They have increased the grants in aid of land owners by four to five millions a year. (5.) They have increased the War Expenditure from 32 millions in 1887 to 35 millions in 1892. .

..... (6.) They have so confused the accounts that it is diffi- cult to tell what is the real income and expenditure in any one year. On the other hand, we have the conversion of the debt; a pitiful reduction of the duties on tea and cur- rants in response to a demand for the abolition of the Breakfast Table Duties ; the reduction of the House Duty, and the reduction of the Income Tax from Bd. to 6d. _

FARM FIRE AT RAINFO RD.

A few minutes before nine o'clock on Wednesday night Detective White, of the St. Helens Railway Station, who had received word by telegraph from Rainford Station, brought word to the St. Helens Town Hall that Burrey House Farm, near Rainford Village, in the occupation of Mr. John Broadman. was in flames. Superintendent Birchall, with 16 or 18 men with steamer and reel, rushed off to the spot, which is about four milea distant, and arrived there by half-past nine. They found the Dutch barn unroofed, and a stack of unthreshed corn and one threshed,in flames, and three other large stacks in the yard consumed. The fire brigade did the best they could with a very poor supply of water, which they got from a pit close by. Being short of water, the brigade at length had to use battering rams to knock the stacks to pieces to save three others. It was about five o'clock on Thursday morning before the brigade could leave. Damage to the extent of over. £4OO was done, but it is covered by insurance.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. A SUCCESSFUL SEASON. _
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. A SUCCESSFUL SEASON. _

The Warrington football season closed on Satur- day, when the match was with Kendal Hornets. Altogether the season has been a very successful one,and Warrington is in a leading position amongst Lancashire clubs as shown by the result of the matches played. D tiring the season 42 matches have been played. 23 being won, 10 lost, and seven drawn,Warrington scoring 255 points to their opponents' 107. Stockport, Broughton Rangers, Kendal Hornets, land Moseley have each succumbed twice to the powers I of the " wirepullers," who have also been victorious over Douglas, Swinton, Brighouse Rangers, Rochdale, St. Clements, Manchester Rangers, Leigh, Widnes, Tyldesley, Barrow, Manchester, Wigan, Lancaster, Leeds Parish Church, nd Broughton. On the other' hand Oldham, St. Helens Recreation and Runcorn ad- ministered defeat to the Warringtonians,whilst Barrow, Broughton, Tyldes/ey, Lancaster, Swinton, and Brig- house Rangers turned the tables on Warrington. The drawn games were with Rochd ale St. Clements, Leeds Parish Church, Manchester, Wigan, Manchester Ran- gers, St. Helens Recreation, and Leigh. The return match with Oldham was cancelled owing to the frost. The scoring was done as follows ,—James Bate 10 tries; Evans seven tries and two dropped goals; Webster seven tries and one dropped goal; Bandies and Jolley live tries each; John Bate and Eleesnm four tries each; Fair. Turner, Ashton, and Thorniley, three each ; I'. R. Lawless three; Donohue, and Berry, two tries; Lawless also having a dropped goal ;T. Barnes one try and one dropped goal; Holmes, Teare,l A. Barnes, Buckley, Westhall, one try each; T. Barnes nine, and Heesora eight goals; Fair. Turner five; Evans two; Munro and John Bate one; Fair. Turner has also placed a penalty goal. The A" Team has done even better than the first team, having won 24 matches, lost five, and drawn one, securing 41 goals, 67 tries, and 96 minors, against 9 goals, 13 tries, and 31 minors. The "A " team have thlls 334 points to their credit, against 74 scored by their opponents. The following are the defeated tgams : Swinton (2), Broughton (2), Widnes (2), llyniesley (2), Mosslev (2), Lancaster (2), Tranmere andemrs, Oldham, St. Helens Recreation, Manchester Rangers, Sutton, Rochdale St. Clements, Manchester, Stockport, anti Failsworth Old Boys. Runcorn twice efeated Warrington, though the constitution of the victors' team was considerably sprinkled with first team men on the first occasion. St-Helens Recreation, Wigan, and Tranmere Wanderers also lowered the Warrington colours. The return match with Stockport was drawn, and fixtures with Thatto Heath, Leigh, Manchester, Sutton, Manchester Rangers, and Oldham wGre cancel- led through stress of weather.

div.head: ft cciTTT THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MA Y 7, 1892. WARRING-TON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION.
div.p: ft cciTTT THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MA Y 7, 1892. WARRING-TON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Temper- ance Federation was held on Thursday evening, at, the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st. The Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) presided, and there were also on platform the Rev. W. J. Adams (Liverpool), Rev. F. K. Freeston, Rev. J. J. Langham, Rev. J. Gunnell, Rev. J. Yonge ; Messrs. W. Roberts, J. Gandy, J. Pemberton, S. B. Stringer, C. Pigot, Councillor Dixon, Sec. There was a good attendance. The meeting lmving been opened with hymn and prayer, Mr. W. RonEnTs, (hon. sec!) read an apology for non-attendance from Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., and a telegram from the Rev. J. Watkins, of Manchester, which stated that he was very ill and could not come. The

BALANCE SHEET which was then read showed as follows :—lncome : Balance from last year, £2 163. 3d. ; subscriptions, £35 183. : special donations, £2l ; bank interest £1 ; total, £59 16s. Expenditure: Grant to the Working- men's Open-air Mission, £5 83. 10d. ; printing, advertis ing. &c., £l4 7s. ; hire of rooms, £1 123. ; sundry ac- counts, £3 1. ; expenses of Brewster Sessions and other legal expenses, £29 Bs. ; balance in the bank, £6 Os. id. (Applause.) He then read the

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE as follows:—" In presenting their annual report the Com- mittee would again rejoice at the satisfactory progress which the temperance movement is making throughout the country. The Warrington Temperance Federation during the past year has done useful work in the town which has not been wanting in good results. A deter- mined effort was made at the

LAST BREWSTER SESSIONS to induce the borough magistrates to reduce the excessive number of licensed houses and also to refuse the grant- ing of any new licenses. The large public meeting held for this purpose was a crowded and enthusiastic ono, and the speeches of our esteemed Rector, and our excellent friends, the Revs. J. Yonge, J. J. Latigham, A. Freeman, and others helped to make the meeting a complete suc- cess. Our magistrates by a small majority renewed the existing licenses, and the licensing committee unani- mously refused all new applications. Your committee determined at the RECENT MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS to question all candidates for municipal honours and tr. ' support those,irrespective ef party politics, who pledged themselves to vote against any person connected with the liquor trade, having a seat upon the Watch Com- mittee. Out ot 18 candidates no less than 12 gave favour- able replies to the question asked of them, arid these 12 candidates including members of both political parties were recommended to the burgesses for election, As the result six of these were elected to seats in the Town Council, and only three were elected who, were opposed to us. At the first meeting of the newly elected Coun- cil a resolution was proposed with the object of exclud- ing a well-known member of the Trade from the Watch Committee. This proposition was supported by all sections of the Council, and your Committee are glad to record that it was carried by a considerable majority. Your Committee has also rendered valuable assistance both financially and otherwise to the WORKING-MEN'S OPEN AIR TEMPERANCE MISSION. whose meetings have been well:attended and a large num- ber of pledges taken. The sell-denying labours of the working-men in holding those meetings in the open air during both summer and winter months are deserving of all praise. It would be a source of encouragern2nt to them if our friends would inaugurate a movement for the provision of a Temperance Hall, the necessity of which must be apparent to all. The experiment of holding

SUNDAY EVENING MEETINGS eller divine service has been tried for a. month and with a fair amount of success, and will justify your Com- mittee in making similar arrangements for nex„4 winter. Help has also been given by members of this Committee in addressing meetings in connection with many of the Bands of Hope within the town and surrounding dis- trict.—Your Committee has heard with satisfaction that the CLAIRE ASPINALL MEMORIAL COMMITTEE propose-.o appoint a Police Court Missionary to attend the courts at Warrington, Widnes, and Newton, and it is earnestly loped that all friends of temperance will contribute liberally to the project. Your committee is anxious to help in securing

nviracrivn TamesnaNce LEGISLATION in the immediate future. The question of Sunday Clos- ing now ripe for settlement, Local Option by means of the direct veto,and the pr.vention of the sale of drink to children, these are planks in our platform far dearer to many of us than party politics. We believe that the accomplishment of these objects is of supreme import- ance to the nation, and it is to be hoped that at the

FORTHCOMING OENBRAL HIACTION no temperance elector will vote for any candidate who will not pledge himself upon thes• questions. In con- clusion your committee, impressed with th• vast import- ance of this work,desires that in the future every one of Us will listen to th• call of duty. As Lady Henry Somerset eloquently says—" It is our call to break the shackles of intemperance, to undo the ill, to crush out the misery, to uplift the fallen, to palliate the suffering, to make the rugged places smooth, and bring the beauty of God's truth to light." With such noble work before us, and with united efforts, may it be our happiness to rejoice in a glorious success."

which had ever characterised that Society, and, apart from party politics, consider what best might be done to promote the cause they had at heart. (Applause.) Having also spoken in favout of Sunday closing, and local option, Mr. Langiram moved a resolution to the effect that as the

SALE OF INTOXICAIING LIQUOR TO CIIILDR7iN was a frightful source of temptation, and tending to corrupt the young and heio them to form criminal habits, the meeting earnestly called upon Parliament to intervene in their behalf by passing without delay the Bill nor before the House of Commons which proposed to make such sale a penal offence. (Applause.) . . . .

, The Rev. J. Yoson, who was received with applause, seconded the motion in a speech vrhith was brief owing to the lateness of the evening. He regarded with pea- sure the great interest that was now being taken in the cause of unprotected children, and spoke with approval of the work of the Soviety for the Prevention of Craelty to Children. He was very glad to see that Liverpool was:taking the lead in respect to preventing the sale of intoxicating liquor to childreu, and he expressed a belief that if the Bill with that object in view was not passed by the present Parliament it would be by the next. (Hear hear, and applause.) The Rev. F. K. FREESTON cordially supported the motion and remarked that if they could alter the drink- ing habits of Englishmen they would not require such societies as that for the prevention of cruelty to children He also suggested that that the Federation should en- deavour to federate all the children's temperance organ- isations and Bands of Hope. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Grtrimr. also briefly supported the motion, after which it was passed unanimouely. The meeting concluded with the singing of the doxology. ELECTION OF OFFICERS, &c.

On Thursday afternoon a meeting of the Committee of the Temperance Federation was held in the Horsemarket st. Cocoa Rooms. The Rector presided, and there was a_ large attendance. The principal business was the appoint ment of officers, who were elected as follows :—President, the Rector; vice-presidents, Revs. J. Yonge, E. Moore' J. J. Langham. F. K. Freeston, J. Gunnell, J. Warnock, J. Dwies, W. Thornley, C. E. Jackson, T. Ross, A. Free- man, E. T. Reed, and J. W. Varley ; Messrs. R. Garnett, S. J. Guest, J. Walker, Councillor H. Roberts, Councillor F. Dixon, H. J. Longton, R. Roberts, J. Dodds, Coun- cillor J. Shaw Green, %V. Twiss, and E. J. Drury ; hon. treasurer, Mr. S. B. Stringer; hen. secretary, Mr. W. Roberts.
SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. EDWARD BREWTNALL.

The death took place suddenly, on Tuesday, oi Mr. E. Brewtnall, editor of the " Warrington Guar- dian." On Friday last week, Mr. Brewtnall was at business, but, not feeling well, he left early in the afternoon for his residence at Didsbury. It was not expected that anything of a serious nature would result from ths, illness,but,on Tuesday morn- ing, a telegram was received at Warrington, an- nouncing that Mr.Brewtnall was dead. Mr.Breivt- nab, at the time of his death, was in his 74th year. He was,we believe, born in Leicestershire. He was originally a schoolmaster, and forty years ago was headmaster of the Warrington People's College, which at that time was in Newton-st.; where the Central Station now sands. He subse- quently went into partnership with Dr. Mac- kie, the proprietor of the " Warrington Guar- dian," and acted as editor for several years. Some time after the firm was turned into a limited company, he retired, but two or three years ago he was again placed in charge of the editorial depart- ment, and continued in it till his death. The de- ceased gentleman took a prominent part in con- nection with the establishment of the Warrington School of Art, and was himself a painter of con- siderable ability. He was a Liberal in politics, and took great interest in educational matters. His son, M. E. F. Brewtnall, has won high distinction in the world of art. lie leaves other three sons and two daughters. The remains of the deceased were yesterday interred at Chorlton-cum-Hardy. The funeral was of a private nature. ,
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday morning at the Town Hall. Mr. H. J. Grice pre- sided and there were present Messrs. IL White, W. Timmins, S. Taylor, W. Hankinson, E. Humphreys, F. Wiswall, W. R. Wass, H. Coward, R. Abel, J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, J. Dobson, J. Meadowcrof r, D. Bisbrown, F. A. Lake (law cleric), E. Marshall (sec.), M. Barker (surveyor.)

THE HEALTH OF TM: TOWN. The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. McDougall) re- ported that during April there were 35 deaths, of which one was an inquest case, and they showed an average death rate of 21 per I,ooo' of the estimated population. Exclusive of the inquest case the death rate was 204. Heart disease caused five deaths and inflammation of the lungs nine deaths.—ln reply to the' Chairman, Dr. McDougall said he could not remember the town being in such a healthy condition as it was at the present time. The Surveyor said in April last year there were ever 39 deaths.

div.head: 2111 CIIAII2IO,N'S ADDAMS.
div.p: 2111 CIIAII2IO,N'S ADDAMS.

The CHAIRMAN said the Committee of the Federation had been so kind as to wish him to again act as president of the Federation this year. Re had had real difficulties to overcome, one of which was connected with the parocial system. That system appointed for them certain boundaries, and he supposed every clergy- man had more than he could properly do within the limits of his own psrish. He did not like to be Chair- man of a society which brought him out of the limits of his own parish. Anether difficulty was one upon which some members of the Federation felt strongly, and that was as to the question of total abstinence, and, as he had always told them, he was not quite a total abstainer himself. Still having deeply at heart the temperance cause and the good of Warrington. and feeling how earn- est the members of the Federation and the Committee were, he could not stand aloof or hang back but must ski his part to help them. (Applause.) Referring to tqueetions in which he felt deeply interested, he said the first and ,foremost was that of Sunday Closing, and then there was the prevention of the sale of liquor to young children. (Applause.) With regard to the proposed appointment of a

POLICE COURT MISSIONARY, he alluded to the generosity of Mr. R. Garnett who had promised £5 a year towards the payment of the mission - ary's salary. As a result of a two days' canvass they had got promises of not far short of £5O per annum towards the same object. (Applause.) The Rev. W. J. ADAMS, of Liverpool, next spoke at some length on the Clarke Aspinall Memorial, and gave many instances of the good that had been done by hay- ing police court missionaries. The Grumman mentioned that it was preposed to give the missionary in this locality £l5O peryinnum.

div.head: R. LANOHAII AND MS- CRITICS.
div.p: R. LANOHAII AND MS- CRITICS.

The Rev. J. J. Lexonam, who was received with ap- plause, said that befere moving the resolution he had to propose he wished to refer to a personal matter. Thai was the tret opportunity he had had of meeting a Warrington audience face to face since some remarks of his and the

action of his friends in connection with the Temperance Federation were misrepresented in the public press, and be wished to take the opportunity of saying how heartily he had been in accord with the entire policy and work of the Warrington Temperance Federation throughout the whole of the year past, how thoroughly he endorsed every word of the report that had been penned by his good friend Mr. Roberts, and how intensely he felt the cruel way in which the action of the Warrington Tem- perance Federation, was, without the slightest justifica- tion, attributed to political motives. (Hear, hear.) The words that he (Mr. Langham) penned in the first instance were simply due to an attack upon himself, an attack which, perhaps, it would have been wiser to have treated with contempt, but an attack which was based upon the asrumed knowledge of the person who uttered the words that he (Mr. Langham) had himself penned his signature to a circular. The whole •f that attack upon himself was based upon that supposition. He wrote to state that it was an erroneous assumption, and upon that, without the slightest justification, the town was placarded with a portion only of his letter—(hear, hear)—misrepresent- ing his own views and misrepresenting the entire action of the Federation. (Hear, hear.) He declined to enter into the matter further in the paper which took it up for the simple reason that what he wrote received editorial comments adverse to himself, and he did not think the treatment fair. (Hear, hear.) Upon that platform THRY KNOW NOTHING OF PARTY POLITICS as such. For his own part he felt very little interest in the modern game of politics. Those questions of Home Rule, of allotments, of small holdings, to his mind were merely insignificant counters useful in the game which ambitious men might like to play. He looked upon the whole question of public politics from the standpoint of a clerayman, and to his mind these petty little questions were entirely overshadowed by the great question of all —what would raise the souls of the people, and what would make them better men. (Applause.)That repre- sented his politics, and such questions as intemperance and gambling, and the way to deal with other sins, should ever stand first and foremost. (Applause.) The only objection that he had to the us• of his name on the circular to which so much reference had been made was simply a feeling of delicacy, that, as a ncn-resident in the borough of Warrington. he had no right to interfere in a Warrington election. But, he was entirely in ac- cord, as he had said before, with all that the Federation had done in the past. (Applause.) He believed that the Federation was doing splendid work, and he hoped it would do a still better work, but if it was to do a still better work in the future than it had done in the past, it must, he believed, adhere to the neutral platform

div.head: SAD DROWNING CASE AT RUNCORN..
div.p: SAD DROWNING CASE AT RUNCORN..

HEARTRENDING SCENE. . A most heartrending accident occurred at Run- corn about four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, when a perambulator, and two babies who were its occupants were thrown into the Big Pool, Heath- road. It appears that Lizzie Sweetman, a girl 15 years of age, daughter of Mr. Matthew Sweetman, coal dealer, Heath-road, took out her baby sister Edith, in a perambulator, and meeting another girl named Jones, in the charge of the latter, a baby aged three, was also placed in the carriage. Oppo- site the Big Pool the girls placed the carriage besides the rail which fences the water, and com- menced to play together, and whilst they were so occupied, the carriage started down the slope, the probablity being that it was set in motion by the wind. The carriage went with incredible speed,. and had rushed into the water before the girl who ran in pursuit could stop it. But she followed on, in her endeavour to save the young lives, and her own was nearly sacrificed to her intrepid conduct. The screams of the girl Jones brought two shipwrights from the boat-building yard of Mr. Samuel Taylor upon the scene. Miss Sweet- man was splashing in the water, and a pole being held out to her by Faulkner she was pulled ashore.. ' The young girl Jones was floating on the water beyond the aid of the pole, and Letter without divesting himself of any clothing plunged into the water, and swam to her rescue. Thinking they had done all that humanity demanded, the men were about to retum to their work, when they were in- forme I there was another baby in the carriage;: the grapnels were cast and by a great effort the perambulator was dragged to land. Sad to relate the baby Sweetman was strapped in the carriage, and her immersion had been for so long a. time that all efforts to restore animation failed. Previous to the grapnels being thrown, bubbles were seen ris- ing to the surface and Letter swam to the spot and dived but failed to secure anything. His gallant conduct is the subject of universal praise, and it is hoped that his bravery will be suitably acknow‘- ledged. THE INQUEST. Mr. J. E. Worsley yesterday held the inquest on the body of Edith Sweetman, at Runcorn Police Court. Mr. S Yarwool was foreman of the jury. The follow- ing evidence was adduced :—Mathew John Sweetman, 2, Malcolm-st., coal dealer, identified the deceased, and said she was ten months old.—Margaret Louisa Arrow- smith, said she was the wife of the Rev.W. Arrowsmith. On Wednesday afternoon she was walking along Heath- road, when she saw the perambulator in what she thought was a very dangerous position. She in- tended to speak to the girl, and tell her that she ought not to leave the carriage. but when she reached her the girl had taken hold of the handle, and appeared about to move away. She therefore passed on without making any remark. After she had walked some distance, she heard is scream, and seeing that something had happened, she returned arui found that the girl and one of the babies had been got out of the water by some men, and she said "There were two babies, have you got them both," The men replied that they did not know there were two, and at once threw in the grappling iron and brought out the perambulator with Mr. Sweetman's baby in it. She helped Mrs. Sweetman to undress the baby, and they used every means to restore animation until Dr. Robin- son arrived, when he also used every exertion, but 'with- out effect. In answer to the Coroner, Mrs. Arrowsmith said the perambulator could easily go under the fencus without the rail touching the children's head. She con- sidered the road at that point very dangerous indeed.— Several jurymen assented. Mary Jane Jones, said her father was John Jones, who was a club collector, and lived in Malcolm-st. She was 12 years of age. She was uith Lizzie Sweetman who had charge of the parainhulator. They placed the perambulator against the railings whilst they played with sticks. They heard the carriage moving and be- fore they col.'d get half way down the " brow " the carriage was in the water. The Ceronor What started it off.—Witness Well there was a lot of wind. Lisale Sweetman jumped in after the perambulator to try to save it. Witness shouted to the men in the dockyard and they came at once. The., elder child, (three years old), who was in the carriage had hold of the rail and both children were knocking their feet against the carriage.—The Coroner : In all human probability that is how the perambulator started. Joseph Faulkner, shipwright, said he lived at Halton. He described hearing screams, and the action he cour- ageouslv took to effect a rescue. Witness said the place where the accident happened was much frequented by children with babies. _ _

The Coroner in.summing up, described the case as very sad one and said the girl was no doubt competent to look 'after a perambulator. It was a plucky thing for the girl to try to sive the perambulator, and he com- mented in terms of great praise upon the brave and gallant conduct of Letter and Faulkner. It was a fool- ish thing for the girl to place the perambulator in so dangerous a p•,sition, but it did not amount to crim- inality. Mr. S. Yarwood maid the jury were unanimous in returning a verdict of accidentally drowned, and also in a recommendation that another rail should be fixed, and they wished the coroner to communicate with the Daresbury Highway Board on the subject.—Mr. Robert Wright said Letter ought not to be neglected.—Mr. Yarwood : It is not the only life he has saved. He is an expert swimmer.—Mr. W. Wright And he is an aged man.—The witness Faulkner said Letter was about 60 years of age and he had been ailing all winter. He was the only man there that could swim.—An effort will be made to (Alain a Human Society's Medal for Letter.

div.head: THU ORDER 07 DEBATE.
div.p: THU ORDER 07 DEBATE.

Mr. Wynne Illimphreys moved that Standing Order X be amended by the addition of the following clause" A member formally seconding any resolution or amend- ment without remarks, and reserving his richt tc, speak, shall not be deemed to have exercised his right to speak upon any such resolution or amendment." Mr. Bisbrown seconded.—Mr. Taylor moved and Mr. Hankinson seconded a direct negative.—Mr. Meadow- croft moved an amendment that the whole of the Stand- ing Orders he referred to the Legal Committee for consid- eration and revision.—Mr. Pritchard seconded.—Mr. Numphreys then withdrew in favour ef ths course suggested by M. Meadowcroft, whose amendment was lost by 9 votes to 5. Mr. Humphreys's motion was then lost by a large majority.

div.head: LIQUOR BILL.
div.p: LIQUOR BILL.

Mr. Bisbrown moved "That the Chairman be autho- rised to affix the seal of the Board to petitions to both Houses of Paliament in favour of the " Sale of Intoxi- cating Liquors to Children," Bill, whereby it is proposed to prohibit the sale or delivery of any description of in- toxicating liquors to any person apparently under the age of 18 years." A letter was read from the Rev. J. S. Simpson,,Bethesda Chapel, informing the Board that a meeting of the representatives, of various temperance societies of the town and district, held on Friday last, passed a resolution asking the Board to take the course asked by Mr. Bisbrown'a motion.—Mr. Bisbrown pointed out that Liverpool Town Council and Board of Guar- dians had adopted a similar resolution, and said the value and necessity of the Bill would not be questioned. The sights seen and the language heard at many of the public-houses was not of a very elevating character, and must have a degrading and baneful influence on the minds of the young people, especially when so many of them had no restraining influence in their own homes. There were many yeung lives blasted through this pernicious practice of getting intoxicating drinks at public-houses. Alluding to the practice of giving sweets to children who fetched liquor, and said he regretted very much that that practice existed in RuncOrn, but he was glad to say to a limited extent. There were publicans and publicans in Runcorn, (hear, hear), and he was proud that the vast majority of them to their eternal credit scorned to do this for the sake of the little gain it would be. Mr. Bisbrown strongly combated the idea that the Board had anything to do with social ques- tions. 'There was not one member who would not risk his life to save a child, and yet here they had the cause of physical and moral death to thousands of our little children,. and he urged that it was the duty of the Board to pass the resolution.—Mr. Pritchard seconded the motion, with the object of discussing whether it came within, the province of the Board to range over all sorts of questions that might be submitted for their considera- tion. Individually he was strongly ia favour of the Bill, but he had his doubt whether he could exercise his authority as a Commissioner, in the matter. He should like some definite line laid down, whether these subjects should be considered or not.—No discussion was raised, however, and the voting showed six for and six against, and the chairman, gave his casting vote against the motion. Mr. Meadowcroft refrained from voting. at a lati!r period of the proceedings the chairman wished to make an explanation with regard to his casting vote, but Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Hump- hreys objected, the former rewkarking that the Chairman had the same opportunity of speaking as the rest of the members, and there was no standing order or rule of debate that gave the Chairman the right to explain his casting vote.—The Chairman said under these circum- stances he must agree that the standing orders needed revisinn.—Mr. P.umphreys said he hoped he would have the courage of his convictions and give notice of motion for a committee to revise them. (Laughter.) The members who voted for the motion were Messrs. Bis- brown, DMsion, Coward, Pritchard, Humphreys and Taylor ; against : The Chairman, Messrs. Wiswall, Abel, Timmins, and Fisher.

AN °BARON PEEL BRIGADE. Mr. Lighttnirn drew a, tendon to the praaticeof throw- , ing orange peel on the parapets of the town, which he said was increasing to an alarming extent,ancl it was so dangerous that something, should he done to prevent it. Neither the police nor the Commissioners had any law by which they could deal with it, and he suggested that the teachers of the various day schools should form their pupils into an orange peel brigade to remove every piece of orange peel they came across on the pin- . pet.—Mr. Taylor said he was sorry that they could not deal with the people who threw it on the footpath.— Eventually, on the motion of Mr. Ilishrown, seconded by Mr. Taylor, it was resolved to issue notices canine- the attention of the public to the danger of the practice 7

div.head: WIDNES KICKING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES KICKING CASE.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr... F. H. Gossage and Mr. J. Birchall, Thomas Griffin,. of Warrington:road, and James Melville and Peter Rylands, of Midwood-st., were charged on .remand with doing grievous bodily harm to Daniel Gilmore, of Midwood-st. Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the prisoners ,asked the Bench to allow the case to drop, as Gilmore was Willing to withdraw on the prisoners mak- ing him.oompensation which they would agree to do.— The magistrates declined to consent to such a course. Theprosecutor deposed that on the 25th of April; hewas going over Lugsdaleßridge,abouteight o'clack at night. Be saw the three prisoners standing by some rail's. .Withbut any warning, Rylands came up to hirn and struck hins on the forehead. Be was also struck.on,the backof the head by one of the other prisoners, He then tried to get over the rails, but Melvin caught hold of him,ancrpulled him back. The other men then caAight bold of his feet and threw him over. There was &deep slope °tithe opposite side of tbe rails. All three prisoners followed him over, and commenced to kick him about thebodys. A man named Patrick McCabe came and lifted him up, He had quarrelled with Rvlandsa week previous to the • assault, but he had not spoken to him,since. He was worse for drink at the time, but had full possession of his senses.—By Mr. Knowles: He did not know how many times he had been to the Assizes and Sessions charged' with wounding. He totally denied thit he struck Rylands first. _

Patrick McCabe, Grove-st., corroborated, and Dr. Olieeffe said Gilmore was out of danger, but, would be unable to do any work for six weeks at least.--Thomas Morris. Fisher-st., stated that Rylands and the prosecu- tor had a fight, and the other prisoners kicked the latter. —P.C. Moore proved arresting prisoners. This completed the case for the prosecution.—Rosa Walsh, 13 years of age,and residing in Leigh-st.,said Gilmore asked Rylands to fight. Then Melvin offered Gilmore a bottle of beer, from which he hal a drink. Ile then threw the bottle down. Rylands got over the rails to go home. Gil- more followed, and they then started to fight.—James Rourke, Alfren-st., said he sact the prisoners and Gil- more fighting. Prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Assizes, bail being allowed.

div.head: TWO CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.
div.p: TWO CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.

A shocking occurrence took place on Thursday morn- ing at the dwelling-house, of some labouring people named Tandy, at Radford Woodhouse, a suburb of Nottingham. A fire broke out in the kitchen in which, at the time three children, aged seven, five and two and, a half, were playing. Before they could be rescued tha two younger were burnt to death, and the elder was so seriously injured that her life is despaired of.

SECRETARY.—WiIIiam Breisford. OsFlcEs.-73, King-street, Manchester. -- THE TRUST FUND SYSTEM. The Directors of the Manchester Trust Limited, recognis- ing the need of other facilities than those already afforded for the investment of money by way of deposit. have decided to give special attention to this class of t usiness. and have taken suitable premises at No. 73, King•st., Manchester, for the purpose. They h :ve accordingly arranged the system of secarity set forth as follows. One of the principal features of the system they have devised is the establishment by trust deed of Specific Trust Funds, whereby. independently of the credit and resources of the Manchester Trust it elf, with its subfcribed capital of £500,000 and reserves, securities at least equal to the amount of the deposits must always be held absolutely charged as security to the depositors. The security thus obtained is of an absolute character, and constitutes for the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment, both as to capital and income, free from all market fluctuations nd vicissitudes • The depositors in each fund will be secured (Firstly).—By a first charge upon the securities lodged in the fund. (Secondly). —By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust Limited. The Manchester Trust Limited will receive on deposit large or 'mad sums (ifot under £10). For sums of £53 or over the Trust will issue certificates in the registered name of the depositor. These will be transfer- able by special transfer form and can he sold and transferred at anytime, like consols, bonds, or shares. Deposits may be for fixed terms, at fixed rates of interest. ,or the Trust will issue certificates, with coupons for the Interest attached payable half-yearly, which may be arranged for special dates. These notes will be re-payable env half- year on seven days' notice. Large sums of over £l,OOO may I If desired, be treated as a ve.cial trust fund, to which specific I securities may be allocated. For sums under £5O (or over that amount if desired for the , convenience of the depositors) pass books will be issued, re- payment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice. The various trust deeds have been settled by connsel,Frank L. Wright, Esq., and can be seen at the offices of the Man- chester Trust, Limited, 73, King-st., Manchester. GENERAL SECURITIES FUND. A.—Certificates for sums of £5O or over will be issued, and Interest allowed in this fund asunder, viz. For six months 4 per cent per annum. For twelve months For two years • 4 per cent per annum. For three years 4l per cent per annum. For deposits withdraWalable at theend of any six months on seven days' notice 4 per cent, per annum. B.—Pass Bo•:ks: For sums under £5O (or over that amount if desired for the convenience of the depositor) pass books will be issued, repayment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice. The rates of interest for fixed terms will be the same as above. For money withdrawable at any time on seven days' notice interest at the rate of 31 per cent per annum will be allowed. THE MORTGAGE SECURITIES FUND. This fund will comprise mortgage securities only. For deposits fixed tor one year and under three years the interest allowed will be 3: per cent, per annum, but if for three years and upwards the rate will be 4 per cent, per annum. -- DEPOSITS ON OPEN ACCOUNT. Moneys (250 or over) will also be received OIL deposit out- side these trust funds on promissory n0t..., as under,— For six months.. For twelve months 4 per cent per annum. For three years and upwards 41 per cent per annum. Full information in respect of any of the before-mentioned funds may be had on apolical ion to the secretary of THE MANCHESTER TRUST LIMITED, WM. ERELSFORD, Secretary. 73, King-street, Manchester,

THISTLETHWAITE. 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, lass. Gentlemen,—l have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke consuming and Fue:-econornising Fires at work continuousl3 in my establishment. One lire has been fixed for fourteer. months, working two large ovens (one heavy cast iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for ihe remainder of the day. The heat olgained from this inferiel coal with this Patent -fire is really marvellous ; mdccl, one can hirdly realise tile tact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge. FIRE AT DOVER RAILWAY STATION. The fire which broke oat in the porters' room at the Senth-Western Railway Station, Dover; on Thursday night, was not subdued till the entire side of the Station - where the offices are situated was burnt out. Ibis damage is estimated at many thousands oPpounds. VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER AGA4NST A STEPMOTHER. Ellen Jane Clark was remanded at the West London Mice 'Mut, yesterday, charged with the manslaughter, oilier step-daughter by a course of ill-treatinent. ,A coroner's jury returned a verdict of ‘" Manslaughter " against the accused on Thursday.. WORK TO BE RESUMED. At I a, meeting of the executive of the Amalgamated ASsociatinn of Operative Cotton Spinners, held at Man- chester yerterday morning, it was unanimously resolved to confirm the arrangement arrived at on Thursday afternoon at the conference of representatives of masters and men. It was also agreed that the men should resume work on Monday morning. - • DARING ROBBERY IN MANCHESTER. • TRAGIC SEQUEL.
